provinces.name: Sicilia
provinces.createdNote: peace of Lutatius 241 BC gave Rome western Sicily; first annual praetor C. Flaminius in 227 BC (Solinus 5.1)
provinces.endedNote: still Roman in 641; lost to the Aghlabids only from 827 (Syracuse 878)
provinces.governor: praetor (from 227 BC); from 27 BC proconsul of praetorian rank; corrector, then consularis (4th c.); praetor from 537 (Justinian, Novel 104)

phases.t: western Sicily ceded by the peace of Lutatius; supervised by a quaestor and ad hoc commanders
praetorian province; Hiero II's kingdom of Syracuse annexed after the siege of 213-211; two quaestors (Syracuse, Lilybaeum)
senatorial province under a proconsul of praetorian rank
province of the diocese of Italia Suburbicaria, corrector then consularis; Vandal raids from 440
Vandal grip loosened; ceded to Odoacer for tribute (c. 476), then Ostrogothic from 491, Roman civil administration intact
taken by Belisarius in 535 without resistance except at Panormus; governed by a praetor reporting to Constantinople rather than to the prefect of Italy

provinces.summary: Rome's first overseas province and the Republic's granary: the lex Hieronica, inherited from Hiero II, took a tithe (decuma) of grain from the cities, auctioned to contractors in Sicily itself. It produced the two great slave wars (135-132 and 104-100 BC) and the most famous extortion case in Roman history, Cicero's prosecution of Verres (governor 73-71). Under the empire it became a land of vast estates; by the 6th century the Roman church's Sicilian patrimony was its richest, and in 641 the island was still securely Roman.

provinces.name: Sardinia (et Corsica)
provinces.createdNote: occupied 238/237 BC; first praetor M. Valerius in 227 BC
provinces.endedNote: still Roman in 641
provinces.governor: praetor (from 227 BC); senatorial proconsul or imperial praefectus/procurator in alternation; praeses (late); praeses and dux under the prefecture of Africa (from 534)

phases.t: seized from Carthage during the Mercenary War; war with the Sardinian tribes
praetorian province of Sardinia with Corsica; revolt of Hampsicora 215; Ti. Gracchus' war 177-176 claimed 80,000 Sards killed or enslaved
senatorial
imperial, under an equestrian praefectus because of brigandage (Dio 55.28.1)
senatorial again in exchange for Nero's freeing of Achaea (Pausanias 7.17.3), then alternating between senatorial and equestrian governors
province of Italia Suburbicaria under a praeses
Vandal (seized c. 456-466); Godas' revolt 533 gave Justinian his opening
recovered 533-534; province of the praetorian prefecture of Africa, a dux at Forum Traiani watching the Barbaricini of the interior

provinces.summary: A malarial, grain-rich island that Rome took by sharp practice in 238 while Carthage was fighting its mercenaries. It was a place of exile and forced labour: Tiberius sent 4,000 freedmen 'infected with Jewish and Egyptian rites' there in AD 19 to fight brigands (Tac. Ann. 2.85), and bishops Pontianus and Hippolytus were deported to its mines in 235. Under Justinian it was run from Carthage, and Gregory the Great's letters show the pagan Barbaricini still unconverted in the 590s.

provinces.name: Corsica
provinces.createdNote: separated from Sardinia under Augustus or soon after; exact date uncertain
provinces.endedNote: still Roman in 641

phases.t: administered with Sardinia; Sullan colony at Aleria and Marian colony at Mariana
separate equestrian province (date of separation uncertain, AD 6 or soon after)
province of Italia Suburbicaria under a praeses
Vandal; a place of exile for Catholic clergy under Huneric
recovered with Sardinia; under the prefecture of Africa

provinces.summary: A poor, mountainous island exporting timber, wax, honey and slaves; Seneca spent his exile there (41-49) and complained of it in verse. Its separation from Sardinia under the early Principate is inferred from equestrian governors attested from the 1st century AD. It remained in Roman hands after 641.

provinces.name: Hispania Citerior (Tarraconensis)
provinces.createdNote: six praetors elected for 197 BC, two for Spain with their boundary fixed (Livy 32.27.6, 32.28.11); first holder C. Sempronius Tuditanus
provinces.endedNote: divided c. 293 into Tarraconensis, Carthaginiensis and Gallaecia
provinces.capitalName: Tarraco (also Carthago Nova in the Republic)
provinces.governor: praetor, usually with proconsular imperium; from 27 BC legatus Augusti pro praetore of consular rank, with three legati iuridici

phases.t: Scipionic war zone against Carthage (provincia without fixed borders)
praetorian province; Celtiberian wars 181-179 and 153-133 (Numantia 133); Sertorius 80-72
imperial Hispania Tarraconensis, enlarged by the northwest after the Cantabrian wars (29-19 BC); legio VII Gemina at Legio from 74

provinces.summary: The largest province of the empire after 19 BC, stretching from the Pyrenees to Galicia. The Republic's longest wars were fought here (the Celtiberians and Numantia, then Sertorius), and its gold, above all the hydraulic mines of Las Medulas, financed the early empire. Seven conventus courts and a provincial cult at Tarraco organised it; Galba was governor when he rose against Nero in 68. Diocletian split it into Tarraconensis, Carthaginiensis and Gallaecia.
provinces.garrison: 2-3 legions under Augustus; VII Gemina alone from 74

provinces.name: Hispania Ulterior
provinces.createdNote: created with Citerior in 197 BC; first praetor M. Helvius
provinces.endedNote: divided under Augustus (27 BC or during 16-13 BC) into Baetica and Lusitania

phases.t: praetorian province of the Guadalquivir valley and the Atlantic west; Lusitanian war 155-139 (Viriathus)

provinces.summary: The rich south: the silver of the Sierra Morena and Rio Tinto, the Phoenician port of Gades, and the Baetis valley. Its governors fought the Lusitanian wars, including the treacherous massacre by Ser. Sulpicius Galba (150) and the war against Viriathus, murdered in 139 by men bribed by Q. Servilius Caepio. Caesar governed it as propraetor in 61-60. Augustus split it into Baetica and Lusitania.

provinces.name: Hispania Baetica
provinces.createdNote: Augustan division of Ulterior, 27 BC or 16-13 BC
provinces.endedNote: Roman government ended with the Suevic capture of Hispalis in 441; Visigothic later; the coast partly Byzantine (Spania) 552-c.624
provinces.governor: proconsul of praetorian rank (senatorial); consularis (4th c.)

phases.t: senatorial province without a legion; four conventus (Gades, Corduba, Astigi, Hispalis)
province of the diocese of Hispaniae under a consularis
Siling Vandals (411-418), Hasding Vandals (to 429), then Sueves (Hispalis 441)

provinces.summary: The most Romanised part of Spain, an exporter of olive oil on an industrial scale: the Dressel 20 amphorae that built Rome's Monte Testaccio came overwhelmingly from the Baetis valley. It produced Trajan and Hadrian (from Italica) and the Senecas (from Corduba), and its Flavian municipal laws (Malaca, Salpensa, Irni) are the best evidence for Roman town charters. Moorish raids in the 170s were its only serious military crisis before the 5th-century invasions.

provinces.name: Lusitania
provinces.createdNote: Augustan division of Ulterior; formalised by 16-13 BC
provinces.endedNote: lost when the Sueves under Rechila took Emerita in 439
provinces.governor: legatus Augusti pro praetore of praetorian rank; consularis (4th c.)

phases.t: imperial province without a legion after the Cantabrian wars; conventus Emeritensis, Pacensis, Scallabitanus
province of the diocese of Hispaniae; Emerita also seat of the vicarius Hispaniarum
Alans (411-418), then Sueves; Rechila took Emerita in 439

provinces.summary: Western Iberia, organised round the veteran colony of Emerita Augusta (25 BC). Its mines (the bronze tablets of Vipasca record the imperial mining code) and the Trajanic bridge at Alcantara are its best-known monuments. Otho governed it for ten years (58-68) as a polite exile after Nero took Poppaea. Emerita was the administrative capital of all Spain in the 4th century.

provinces.name: Gallia Transalpina / Narbonensis
provinces.createdNote: campaigns of 122-121 BC; Narbo founded 118 BC; continuous governorship well attested only from the 70s (M. Fonteius c. 75-73)
provinces.endedNote: divided by Diocletian into Narbonensis I, Narbonensis II and Viennensis
provinces.governor: proconsul in the Republic (often held with Cisalpina); imperial legate 27-22 BC; then proconsul of praetorian rank

phases.t: Gallia Transalpina, conquered after the defeat of the Allobroges and Arverni (121); Via Domitia; colony at Narbo 118
imperial
senatorial Gallia Narbonensis (Dio 54.4.1)

provinces.summary: The 'Provincia' (Provence): the land link between Italy and Spain, secured by Cn. Domitius Ahenobarbus' road. The Cimbri and Teutones annihilated two consular armies at Arausio here in 105 before Marius destroyed the Teutones at Aquae Sextiae in 102. Caesar's base for the conquest of Gaul; in Pliny's phrase 'more truly Italy than a province' (NH 3.31), with veteran colonies at Arelate, Forum Iulii, Baeterrae and Arausio. Massilia remained a free ally until Caesar took it in 49.

provinces.name: Gallia Cisalpina
provinces.createdNote: regular province conventionally dated to Sulla (c. 81 BC); earlier a frequent but not continuous command; the date is debated
provinces.endedNote: absorbed into Italy by the triumvirs in 42 BC, effective 41
provinces.capitalName: no fixed seat (Placentia, Mutina, Ravenna used)
provinces.governor: proconsul (Caesar 59-49 BC, with Illyricum and Transalpina)

phases.t: Gallic war zone and recurrent praetorian provincia; Latin colonies Placentia and Cremona 218, Bononia 189
regular province, usually dated to Sulla; Transpadanes Latin after the lex Pompeia of 89
citizenship for the Transpadanes (lex Roscia 49); merged into Italy, effective 41

provinces.summary: The Po valley, the Republic's great colonial frontier and later its recruiting ground: Caesar raised most of his Gallic legions here. Its southern boundary on the Rubicon made a river crossing in January 49 an act of war. The Mutina campaign of 43 was fought on its roads. After 42 it simply became part of Italy.

provinces.name: Gallia Comata (Caesar's conquest)
provinces.endedNote: organised into Aquitania, Lugdunensis and Belgica (27 BC; completed 16-13 BC)
provinces.capitalName: none; Augustus held a conventus at Narbo in 27 BC
provinces.governor: proconsul of Transalpina and his legates

phases.t: conquered by Caesar
administered loosely from Narbonensis; tribute fixed at 40 million sesterces a year (Suetonius, Iul. 25)

provinces.summary: 'Long-haired Gaul', the territory Caesar conquered between 58 and 51. It paid a light tribute and was governed almost informally until Augustus' census of 27 BC and his long stay of 16-13 BC organised it into three provinces, crowned by the Altar of Rome and Augustus at Lugdunum (12 BC).

provinces.name: Illyricum
provinces.createdNote: as a regular command from 59 BC; its earlier status as a province is debated
provinces.endedNote: divided c. AD 9 into Dalmatia and Pannonia
provinces.governor: proconsul (Caesar 59-49 BC); senatorial proconsul 27-11 BC; imperial legate from 11 BC

phases.t: Roman protectorate along the Adriatic coast after the Illyrian wars (229, 219, 168)
provincia of Caesar by the lex Vatinia; Octavian's Illyrian war 35-33 (wounded at Metulum)
senatorial province
imperial; Tiberius' Pannonian war 12-9 BC; Great Illyrian Revolt (Bato) AD 6-9

provinces.summary: The Adriatic coast and its hinterland, a provincia long before it was an organised province. The great revolt of AD 6-9, which Suetonius called the most serious foreign war since Hannibal, tied down ten legions under Tiberius. After it the region was split into Dalmatia (Illyricum Superius) and Pannonia (Illyricum Inferius).

provinces.name: Macedonia
provinces.createdNote: defeat of Andriscus by Q. Caecilius Metellus Macedonicus 148 BC; settlement by ten commissioners 146 BC
provinces.endedNote: Thessalonica and the coast still Roman in 641; much of the interior under Slav sklaviniai from c. 580-620
provinces.governor: proconsul (Republic); senatorial proconsul of praetorian rank; under the legate of Moesia AD 15-44; consularis (late)

phases.t: four autonomous merides after Pydna
province after Andriscus' defeat by Metellus (148); front against Thracians, Scordisci and Dardani; Via Egnatia built c. 146-120
senatorial
imperial, joined with Achaea and Moesia under one legate (Poppaeus Sabinus 15-35)
senatorial again (Claudius)
Macedonia (Prima), diocese of Moesiae then Macedonia; Thessalonica seat of the prefect of Illyricum from the 5th century

provinces.summary: The Republic's eastern bastion, with the Via Egnatia running from Dyrrachium to Thessalonica. Its governors fought endless border wars and some were notorious, like L. Calpurnius Piso (57-55), whom Cicero savaged in In Pisonem. Brutus and Cassius made their last stand at Philippi in 42. In late antiquity Thessalonica became the capital of eastern Illyricum and survived the Avar and Slav sieges of 586 and 615-618 under the protection, its citizens believed, of St Demetrius.

provinces.name: Achaea
provinces.createdNote: supervised from Macedonia after 146 BC; separate province 27 BC
provinces.endedNote: still Roman in 641, though much of the Peloponnese interior was settled by Slavs from the 580s (Chronicle of Monemvasia)
provinces.governor: proconsul of praetorian rank; proconsul (late, outside the vicar's control)

phases.t: Greece supervised by the governor of Macedonia after Mummius' sack of Corinth; many free and allied cities
senatorial province
imperial, with Macedonia and Moesia
senatorial
declared free by Nero at the Isthmus (28 Nov 67); freedom revoked by Vespasian
senatorial; Hadrian's Panhellenion (131/2) centred on Athens
proconsular province of the diocese of Macedonia; Heruli 267, Alaric 395-396, Slav settlement from the 580s

provinces.summary: Old Greece south of Thessaly, run from Caesar's colony at Corinth rather than from Athens. Its proconsul L. Iunius Gallio (51-52), Seneca's brother, dismissed the Jews' case against Paul; the Delphi inscription naming him anchors Pauline chronology. Nero's theatrical grant of freedom in 67 lasted only a few years. In late antiquity it was one of only three provinces under a proconsul, a mark of prestige rather than power.

provinces.name: Epirus (Vetus)
provinces.endedNote: still Roman in 641 along the coast; interior affected by Slav settlement

phases.t: devastated by Aemilius Paullus in 167 (70 towns sacked, 150,000 enslaved); under Macedonia
part of Achaea
separate procuratorial province, created under Trajan (date approximate)
Epirus Vetus, diocese of Moesiae then Macedonia; Epirus Nova split off to the north

provinces.summary: A land never recovered from Rome's punitive enslavement of 167 BC, when on a single day the Senate's order was carried out across seventy towns. Octavian's victory city of Nicopolis (founded after Actium, 31 BC) became its capital and the home of Epictetus' school. It became a separate equestrian province under Trajan, and in late antiquity a modest Greek province on the edge of the Slav settlements.

provinces.name: Asia
provinces.createdNote: Attalus III died 133 BC; province organised 129-126 BC
provinces.endedNote: divided c. 293 into Asia (proconsularis), Hellespontus, Lydia, Caria, Phrygia I-II and Insulae
provinces.governor: praetor or proconsul (Republic); proconsul of consular rank (senatorial)

phases.t: bequeathed by Attalus III; war against Aristonicus
organised by M'. Aquillius 129-126; tithe farmed out in Rome by the lex Sempronia of 123
overrun by Mithridates VI; the 'Asian Vespers' killed 80,000 Romans and Italians
Sulla's indemnity of 20,000 talents; publicani and debt crisis; Lucullus' relief measures
senatorial, the most prestigious proconsulship with Africa
reduced: Caria et Phrygia separated (c. 250)

provinces.summary: The richest province of the Republic and the jewel of the senatorial career: Josephus speaks of its five hundred cities. Gaius Gracchus' tax law turned it into a hunting ground for equestrian publicani, which helps explain why in 88 the cities joined Mithridates in killing every Italian they could find. Under the empire it was a world of competitive civic building, imperial cult (the koinon of Asia, the calendar decree of 9 BC) and rhetoric. Diocletian cut it into seven provinces.

provinces.name: Bithynia et Pontus
provinces.createdNote: bequest of Nicomedes IV (died late 75 or 74 BC)
provinces.endedNote: divided c. 293 into Bithynia, Paphlagonia and Diospontus
provinces.governor: proconsul; special imperial legates under Trajan; imperial legate from Hadrian

phases.t: Bithynia, bequeathed by Nicomedes IV; Third Mithridatic War
Bithynia et Pontus, organised by the lex Pompeia with eleven city territories in western Pontus
senatorial; Pliny the Younger sent as special consular legate c. 110-112
imperial, Hadrian taking it in exchange for Lycia-Pamphylia (Dio 69.14.4)

provinces.summary: A province of quarrelsome, overspending Greek cities, made famous by Pliny's tenth book of letters: Trajan forbade Nicomedia a 150-man fire brigade for fear of political clubs, and Pliny asked how to treat Christians. Pompey's law of 63 fixed its civic constitutions for centuries. Diocletian made Nicomedia an imperial capital, and the Great Persecution began there in 303.

provinces.name: Cilicia
provinces.createdNote: M. Antonius received Cilicia as a provincia in 102 BC; a territorial province from c. 80 BC
provinces.endedNote: split under Diocletian into Cilicia and Isauria
provinces.governor: praetor/proconsul (Republic); part of Syria under Augustus; imperial legate of praetorian rank from 72

phases.t: anti-pirate command of M. Antonius (102), then a territorial province of Pamphylia, Pisidia and Lycaonia (Dolabella 80-79; Servilius Isauricus 78-74)
enlarged by Pompey with Cilicia Pedias; Cicero governor 51-50, also over Cyprus and three Phrygian assize districts
plain Cilicia attached to Syria; Rough Cilicia left to client kings (Archelaus, Antiochus IV of Commagene)
separate imperial province created by Vespasian, including Rough Cilicia; later its governor also had Isauria and Lycaonia

provinces.summary: Born as a pirate war, Cilicia became a territorial province by stages. Cicero's governorship (51-50) is documented day by day in his letters: he took Pindenissus, was hailed imperator, and refused to help Brutus collect a loan at 48 percent from Salamis on Cyprus. Paul was a citizen of Tarsus. Vespasian made it a province in its own right in 72.

provinces.name: Cyrene
provinces.endedNote: joined with Crete as Creta et Cyrenaica (by 27 BC)
provinces.governor: quaestor pro praetore (74 BC); later proconsul

phases.t: bequeathed by Ptolemy Apion; Rome took the royal lands, the cities left free
organised as a province by P. Cornelius Lentulus Marcellinus; Antony gave it to Cleopatra Selene 34-30

provinces.summary: Ptolemy Apion's bequest of 96 was accepted but neglected for two decades; only the grain crisis and pirate war of the 70s led Rome to send a quaestor in 74. Cyrenaica's famous export, silphium, was nearly extinct by the 1st century AD (Pliny says the last stalk was sent to Nero).

provinces.name: Creta
provinces.endedNote: still Roman in 641; lost to Andalusian Arabs c. 824-827

phases.t: conquered by Q. Caecilius Metellus Creticus 69-67; administered with Cyrene
part of the senatorial province of Creta et Cyrenaica
separate province of the diocese of Moesiae, then Macedonia; the great earthquake of 21 July 365 wrecked Gortyn

provinces.summary: The pirates' island, whose archers served every Hellenistic army. M. Antonius Creticus (father of the triumvir) lost a fleet to the Cretans in 72-71; Metellus needed three years of sieges to subdue them. Gortyn, with its archaic law code and a large Roman praetorium, was the capital. The island stayed Roman until the Andalusian Arab conquest of the 820s.

provinces.name: Creta et Cyrenaica
provinces.endedNote: divided c. 297 into Creta, Libya Superior and Libya Inferior
provinces.governor: proconsul of praetorian rank, with a legate and a quaestor

phases.t: senatorial; Augustus' Cyrene edicts (7/6 and 4 BC) regulate juries and extortion trials
Jewish diaspora revolt (Lukuas/Andreas) devastates Cyrene
Hadrianic restoration of Cyrene; refoundation of the city's temples and colonists sent

provinces.summary: An awkward pairing of two regions separated by 300 km of sea. The five Cyrene edicts of Augustus, found in 1926, are a key text for provincial justice, including the senatus consultum Calvisianum of 4 BC on extortion procedure. The revolt of 115-117 is recorded in inscriptions of Hadrian rebuilding roads and baths 'destroyed in the Jewish tumult'.

provinces.name: Syria
provinces.createdNote: Pompey deposed Antiochus XIII in 64 BC; first governor M. Aemilius Scaurus
provinces.endedNote: split by Septimius Severus in 194 into Syria Coele and Syria Phoenice
provinces.governor: proconsul (Republic; first consular governor Gabinius 57-54); imperial legate of consular rank

phases.t: annexed by Pompey; Crassus destroyed at Carrhae 53; Parthian invasion of Pacorus and Labienus 41-38
imperial, the senior eastern command with 3-4 legions; client states (Commagene, Emesa, Ituraea) absorbed in the 1st century

provinces.summary: The great eastern command, facing Parthia from Antioch. Its legate was the most powerful man in the East: Quirinius ran the census of AD 6, Corbulo and Mucianus made and unmade emperors, and Avidius Cassius proclaimed himself emperor in 175. After Pescennius Niger's bid in 193-194 Septimius Severus split it in two so that no single governor would command so many legions.
provinces.garrison: III Gallica, IV Scythica, VI Ferrata, X Fretensis (to 66), XII Fulminata (to 70), XVI Flavia Firma (from 72)

provinces.name: Cyprus
provinces.createdNote: lex Clodia 58 BC; annexation by M. Porcius Cato 58-56 BC
provinces.endedNote: still Roman in 641; first Arab invasion 649
provinces.governor: attached to Cilicia (Republic); imperial 30-22 BC; proconsul of praetorian rank; consularis (late)

phases.t: annexed under the lex Clodia; Cato liquidated the royal treasure (7,000 talents)
returned to Ptolemaic rule by Caesar and Antony
imperial
senatorial; Jewish revolt 116-117
province of the diocese of Oriens; church autocephalous after Ephesus 431
part of Justinian's quaestura exercitus (Novel 41)

provinces.summary: Annexed in 58 so that Clodius could pay for free grain, Cyprus was run by Cato, who shipped the treasure of Ptolemy of Cyprus to Rome. Its copper mines (Soli) were leased by Herod the Great. Sergius Paullus, proconsul, met Paul and Barnabas at Paphos (Acts 13). In the revolt of 116-117 Dio claims 240,000 Greeks were killed and Jews were afterwards barred from the island.

provinces.name: Africa (Vetus, then Proconsularis)
provinces.createdNote: Carthage destroyed by Scipio Aemilianus 146 BC
provinces.endedNote: divided c. 293-303 into Africa Proconsularis (Zeugitana), Byzacena and Tripolitania

phases.t: Africa (Vetus) behind the Fossa Regia, governed from Utica; Gracchan colony Iunonia (122); Jugurthine War 111-105
beside Africa Nova; Caesar's colony at Carthage (44)
senatorial, the only senatorial province with a legion (III Augusta); war with Tacfarinas 17-24
the legion's legate takes over military command (Caligula); Gordian I proclaimed at Thysdrus 238

provinces.summary: Carthage's territory, annexed after its destruction in 146 and expanded into the grain and olive belt of the Maghreb. By Nero's day Josephus says Africa fed Rome for eight months of the year. It was the last senatorial province to command a legion, until Caligula transferred the legion to an imperial legate in 39. Diocletian reduced it to the hinterland of Carthage.

provinces.name: Africa Nova
provinces.endedNote: merged with Africa Vetus into Africa Proconsularis between c. 36 and 27 BC

phases.t: the eastern kingdom of Juba I, annexed after Thapsus; Cirta and its district given to P. Sittius

provinces.summary: Caesar's annexation of Juba I's kingdom after Thapsus. Its first governor was the historian Sallust, who enriched himself so blatantly (Dio 43.9) that he retired to build the Horti Sallustiani and write about other men's corruption.

provinces.name: Aegyptus
provinces.createdNote: Octavian took Alexandria on 1 August 30 BC
provinces.endedNote: divided c. 297-314 into Aegyptus Iovia, Aegyptus Herculia and Thebais (with the Libyas)
provinces.governor: praefectus Aegypti (equestrian); senators barred from entering without imperial leave

phases.t: prefecture; Cornelius Gallus first prefect (30-26); nomes under strategoi, three or four epistrategiai
Severus grants councils to Alexandria and the nome capitals (200/201); revolts of Firmus (272) and Domitius Domitianus (297-298)

provinces.summary: Egypt was the emperor's own preserve, governed by an equestrian prefect and closed to senators (Tac. Ann. 2.59), because whoever held it held Rome's bread. The papyri make it the best-documented province of the empire, from tax receipts to village lawsuits. The first prefect, the poet Cornelius Gallus, boasted of his deeds on a trilingual stele at Philae and was forced to suicide in 26 BC. Diocletian besieged Alexandria for eight months in 297-298 and then divided the country.
provinces.garrison: 3 legions under Augustus; then III Cyrenaica and XXII Deiotariana; II Traiana alone from the 120s

provinces.name: Galatia
provinces.endedNote: Diocletian reduced it to the old Galatian heartland; Pisidia, Lycaonia (later), Paphlagonia separated
provinces.governor: imperial legate of praetorian rank; consular legate when joined with Cappadocia (72-c.113)

phases.t: the kingdom of Amyntas, enlarged with Pisidia, Lycaonia, Paphlagonia (6 BC), Pontus Galaticus and (64) Pontus Polemoniacus
part of the combined Galatia-Cappadocia
separate again under a praetorian legate

provinces.summary: A vast composite province built from the kingdom of Amyntas after he died fighting the Homonadeis in 25 BC. The Augustan colonies at Pisidian Antioch, Lystra and elsewhere were planted to police the Taurus. The temple of Rome and Augustus at Ancyra preserves the fullest text of Augustus' Res Gestae in Latin and Greek. Paul's 'Galatians' may be the Celts of the north or the cities of the southern province.

provinces.name: Galatia-Cappadocia (Flavian combined command)
provinces.endedNote: Trajan split it, between c. 107 and 113
provinces.governor: legatus Augusti pro praetore of consular rank

phases.t: Vespasian's combined eastern command, with legions at Satala and Melitene

provinces.summary: After Corbulo's Armenian wars Vespasian created a new consular command on the upper Euphrates, uniting Galatia, Cappadocia, Pontus and Armenia Minor under one legate with two legions (XII Fulminata at Melitene, XVI Flavia Firma at Satala, later XV Apollinaris). Trajan separated Galatia again around the time of his Parthian war.

provinces.name: Cappadocia
provinces.endedNote: reduced and divided under Diocletian; Pontic and Armenian districts separated
provinces.governor: equestrian procurator (17-72); consular legate with two legions (from c. 113)

phases.t: procuratorial province after the death of king Archelaus in Rome
part of Galatia-Cappadocia
consular legate on the Euphrates frontier; Armenia Minor and Pontus Polemoniacus attached; Arrian governor 131-137

provinces.summary: Tiberius summoned old king Archelaus to Rome, where he died, and annexed his kingdom in 17, halving the 1 percent sales tax at Rome on the strength of its revenue (Tac. Ann. 2.42). Later the consular legate of Cappadocia guarded the upper Euphrates: Arrian's Periplus of the Black Sea and his order of battle against the Alans (135) are reports from this post. Shapur I took Caesarea in 260.
provinces.garrison: XII Fulminata (Melitene), XV Apollinaris or XVI Flavia Firma (Satala)

provinces.name: Lycia et Pamphylia
provinces.createdNote: Lycia annexed AD 43; Pamphylia joined to it under Vespasian (c. 74)
provinces.endedNote: divided c. 300 into Lycia and Pamphylia
provinces.capitalName: no single seat (Patara and Xanthos in Lycia; Perge and Attaleia in Pamphylia)
provinces.governor: imperial legate (Lycia from 43; combined from c. 74); proconsul from c. 135

phases.t: Lycia annexed by Claudius after civil strife (Dio 60.17.3); Q. Veranius first legate
Lycia et Pamphylia, imperial (Vespasian)
senatorial, exchanged for Bithynia

provinces.summary: Claudius ended the independence of the Lycian League, whose federal constitution with cities voting by size (three, two or one votes) Strabo admired. The Stadiasmus Patarensis, a pillar listing the roads Veranius built across Lycia in 45-46, is the oldest Roman road inventory in Asia Minor. In the 2nd century Lycian benefactors like Opramoas of Rhodiapolis rebuilt whole cities after the earthquake of 141.

provinces.name: Gallia Aquitania
provinces.endedNote: divided under Diocletian into Aquitanica I, Aquitanica II and Novempopulana
provinces.governor: legatus Augusti pro praetore of praetorian rank

phases.t: imperial province from the Pyrenees to the Loire; no legion

provinces.summary: Augustus deliberately joined the Iberian-speaking Aquitani of the southwest with fourteen Celtic peoples up to the Loire. A wealthy, unwarlike province of villas, it is best known for the Hasparren inscription in which a local notable boasts of getting the Nine Peoples separated from the Gauls, the origin of Novempopulana.

provinces.name: Gallia Lugdunensis
provinces.endedNote: divided under Diocletian into Lugdunensis I and II; later III and Senonia
provinces.governor: legatus Augusti pro praetore of praetorian rank

phases.t: imperial province from Lugdunum to Armorica; urban cohort (XIII Urbana) guarding the mint at Lugdunum

provinces.summary: Lugdunum was the de facto capital of all three Gauls: the Altar of Rome and Augustus at the confluence (12 BC) hosted the annual council of sixty Gallic civitates, and the city held an imperial mint. Claudius, born there, made his speech for admitting Gallic nobles to the Senate in 48 (the Lyon Tablet). C. Iulius Vindex, governor in 68, began the rising that brought down Nero, and the battle of Lugdunum (197) between Severus and Clodius Albinus was the largest Roman battle in Gaul.

provinces.name: Gallia Belgica
provinces.endedNote: divided under Diocletian into Belgica I and II
provinces.capitalName: Durocortorum (Reims); financial procurator at Augusta Treverorum
provinces.governor: legatus Augusti pro praetore of praetorian rank

phases.t: imperial; the Rhine army districts formally within it
after the creation of the two Germanies, the civilian hinterland of the Rhine

provinces.summary: The supply base of the Rhine armies, whose procurator at Trier also handled the finances of both Germanies. In 70 the Treveran nobles Classicus and Tutor joined Civilis to proclaim an 'Empire of the Gauls', which collapsed within months. In the 3rd century Trier became the capital of the Gallic Empire and later of Constantius I.

provinces.name: Germania (Augustan province east of the Rhine)
provinces.createdNote: Velleius 2.97 and 2.117-118; Dio 56.18 describe provincial organisation after Tiberius' campaigns of 8-7 BC
provinces.endedNote: abandoned after the Varian disaster, September AD 9
provinces.capitalName: Ara Ubiorum (Oppidum Ubiorum) as cult centre

phases.t: conquest by Drusus (12-9 BC) and Tiberius (8-7 BC)
province in the making: markets, a civil settlement with forum at Waldgirmes, tribute and Roman jurisdiction under Varus

provinces.summary: Velleius and Dio describe a Germany being turned into a province, and the excavation of Waldgirmes (Lahn valley), a planned town with a forum and a gilded bronze equestrian statue of Augustus, proved them right. Varus' imposition of tribute and courts provoked Arminius' ambush in the Teutoburg Forest (AD 9), destroying legions XVII, XVIII and XIX. Germanicus' campaigns (14-16) avenged it but Tiberius never tried to restore the province.

provinces.name: Germania Superior
provinces.createdNote: formally a province by c. 83-90 (Domitian); its legate is attested as provincial governor from the 90s
provinces.endedNote: divided under Diocletian into Germania I and Maxima Sequanorum
provinces.governor: legatus Augusti pro praetore of consular rank

phases.t: military district of the exercitus Germanicus superior within Belgica
province; Saturninus' revolt at Mogontiacum (January 89); Upper German-Raetian limes advanced c. 160
the Agri Decumates beyond the Rhine lost under Gallienus

provinces.summary: Domitian turned the two Rhine army commands into provinces after his Chattan war. The upper province included the Agri Decumates and, from the 160s, the Odenwald-Neckar and outer limes with their palisade and ditch. The appendix to the Verona List records the civitates lost beyond the Rhine under Gallienus around 260.
provinces.garrison: XXII Primigenia (Mogontiacum), VIII Augusta (Argentorate); XI Claudia at Vindonissa to 101

provinces.name: Germania Inferior
provinces.endedNote: became Germania II under Diocletian
provinces.governor: legatus Augusti pro praetore of consular rank

phases.t: military district of the exercitus Germanicus inferior within Belgica; Batavian revolt 69-70
province with the Lower Rhine fleet (classis Germanica)
heartland of the Gallic Empire (Postumus proclaimed at Cologne, 260)

provinces.summary: The Lower Rhine command, where Vitellius was proclaimed emperor in January 69 and where the Batavian revolt of Civilis besieged Vetera in 69-70. The Lower Rhine never had a wall: the river itself, with its forts and fleet, was the frontier. Postumus created the Gallic Empire here in 260.
provinces.garrison: XXX Ulpia Victrix (Vetera), I Minervia (Bonna); four legions before 70

provinces.name: Britannia
provinces.createdNote: Claudian invasion under A. Plautius, AD 43
provinces.endedNote: divided into Superior and Inferior (Herodian dates it to 197; epigraphy suggests completion c. 213)
provinces.governor: legatus Augusti pro praetore of consular rank

phases.t: Claudian conquest; Camulodunum colony (49); Boudica's revolt destroys Camulodunum, Londinium and Verulamium (60/61)
Flavian advance to Scotland; Agricola's victory at Mons Graupius (83 or 84); Inchtuthil abandoned c. 87
Hadrian's Wall (122); Antonine Wall (142-c.160); Clodius Albinus' bid for empire 193-197

provinces.summary: A province that cost more than it paid, Strabo had predicted, and held a garrison out of all proportion to its size: three legions and perhaps 50,000 troops. Tacitus' Agricola is a biography of one of its governors and a meditation on what conquest meant ('they make a desert and call it peace'). Its governors were dangerous because of their armies, which is why Severus or Caracalla split it.
provinces.garrison: II Augusta, IX Hispana (to c. 108+), XIV Gemina (to 66), XX Valeria Victrix, II Adiutrix (c. 71-87), VI Victrix (from 122)

provinces.name: Britannia Superior
provinces.createdNote: Herodian 3.8.2 places the division in 197; dated by many to c. 213-216
provinces.endedNote: reorganised after Constantius I recovered Britain in 296
provinces.governor: legatus Augusti pro praetore of consular rank

phases.t: southern province with legions at Isca and Deva
under Carausius and Allectus

provinces.summary: The southern half of the divided island, with two legions, II Augusta at Isca and XX Valeria Victrix at Deva. Its coast received the first forts of what became the Saxon Shore system in the later 3rd century.

provinces.name: Britannia Inferior
provinces.endedNote: reorganised after 296
provinces.governor: legatus Augusti pro praetore of praetorian rank (also legate of VI Victrix)

phases.t: northern province, Hadrian's Wall and VI Victrix at Eboracum
under Carausius and Allectus

provinces.summary: The northern province, garrisoning Hadrian's Wall; Septimius Severus died at York in February 211 after his Caledonian campaigns. Its governor commanded only one legion, by design.

provinces.name: Raetia (et Vindelicia)
provinces.endedNote: divided c. 290-300 into Raetia I and II
provinces.governor: praefectus, then equestrian procurator; praetorian legate commanding III Italica from c. 179

phases.t: conquered by Drusus and Tiberius in 15 BC; procuratorial, auxiliary garrison; Raetian limes
legio III Italica at Castra Regina; Raetian limes rebuilt as a stone wall c. 200-210; Alamannic invasions 213, 233, 260
the limes abandoned for the Danube-Iller-Rhine line

provinces.summary: The Alpine conquest of 15 BC is commemorated by the Tropaeum Alpium at La Turbie, listing forty-five subdued peoples. In 1992 an altar found at Augsburg recorded the governor's victory on 24-25 April 260 over the Semnones or Iuthungi, who were returning from Italy with thousands of captives, a rare dated document of the 3rd-century crisis.

provinces.name: Noricum
provinces.createdNote: annexed 16 BC after the Norici joined a raid on Istria (Dio 54.20.2)
provinces.endedNote: divided c. 293-300 into Noricum Ripense and Noricum Mediterraneum
provinces.governor: equestrian procurator; praetorian legate commanding II Italica from the 170s

phases.t: the Celtic regnum Noricum absorbed peacefully (16 BC); procuratorial; Claudian municipia
Marcomannic wars; legio II Italica at Lauriacum; governor's seat at Ovilava

provinces.summary: A client kingdom long tied to Roman merchants through its iron (ferrum Noricum, the best steel of antiquity) and gold, absorbed without a war. The Magdalensberg trading post, whose walls bear Latin graffiti listing iron shipments, predates the province. The Marcomannic wars brought it a legion and a senatorial governor.

provinces.name: Alpes Maritimae
provinces.createdNote: conquest of the Ligurian Alpine peoples, 14 BC
provinces.endedNote: ceded with Provence to the Visigoth Euric (476); northern districts Burgundian

phases.t: procuratorial; Latin rights granted by Nero in 63 (Tac. Ann. 15.32)
province of the diocese of Viennensis (Septem Provinciae)

provinces.summary: The mountain hinterland of Nice and the Via Iulia Augusta, conquered in 14 BC and celebrated by the Tropaeum Alpium (7/6 BC) above Monaco. In 69 its procurator Marius Maturus armed the mountaineers for Vitellius against Otho's fleet (Tac. Hist. 2.12-15).

provinces.name: Alpes Cottiae (Alpine province)
provinces.endedNote: name transferred under Diocletian to a province of Italia Annonaria

phases.t: client realm of Cottius, made praefectus civitatium; arch at Segusio (9/8 BC); Claudius restored the royal title to Cottius II
procuratorial province annexed by Nero on the death of Cottius II

provinces.summary: Cottius kept his mountain kingdom by building the road over the Mont Genevre and accepting a Roman title; his arch at Susa lists the fourteen communities he ruled. Nero annexed it in 63 (Suet. Nero 18). Diocletian moved the name to a new Italian province in the Ligurian Apennines.

provinces.name: Alpes Poeninae (Vallis Poenina)
provinces.endedNote: joined with Alpes Graiae under one procurator by the later 2nd century

phases.t: the Valais, attached to Raetia
separate procuratorial district under Claudius (date approximate)

provinces.summary: The upper Rhone valley and the Great St Bernard pass (Summus Poeninus), turned by Claudius into a procuratorial district with a new market town at Martigny. Joined with the Alpes Graiae under one procurator by the later 2nd century.

provinces.name: Alpes Graiae (Atrectianae)
provinces.endedNote: merged into Alpes Graiae et Poeninae

phases.t: procuratorial district of the Ceutrones of the Tarentaise (Claudian)

provinces.summary: The Tarentaise valley and the Little St Bernard pass (Alpis Graia), home of the Ceutrones; a small procuratorial district, merged with the Valais under one procurator by the later 2nd century.

provinces.name: Alpes Graiae et Poeninae
provinces.createdNote: the two districts under one procurator by c. 180 (approximate)
provinces.endedNote: absorbed by the Burgundian kingdom in the 460s-470s

phases.t: single procuratorial province
province of the diocese of Galliae (Verona List)

provinces.summary: Two Alpine passes, the Great and Little St Bernard, joined as one small province commanding the routes from Italy into Gaul. The Burgundians, settled in Sapaudia in 443, absorbed it in the later 5th century.

provinces.name: Dalmatia
provinces.endedNote: Salona fell to Avars and Slavs c. 614 (traditional date; perhaps 620s); coastal towns (Iader, Tragurium, Spalatum) remained Roman

phases.t: Illyricum Superius, later Dalmatia; legions VII and XI (Claudia pia fidelis after refusing Scribonianus' revolt, 42)
unarmed province; rich silver and gold mines in the interior
province of the diocese of Pannoniae/Illyricum; Praevalitana separated; Diocletian's palace at Spalatum
semi-independent under Marcellinus and then Julius Nepos (died 480)
Odoacer, then the Ostrogoths (from 493)
recovered by Justinian (535-537); overwhelmed by Avars and Slavs in the early 7th century

provinces.summary: After the great revolt of AD 6-9 Dalmatia was held by two legions until Domitian moved them to the Danube. It was a reservoir of soldiers and emperors (Diocletian retired to his palace at Split in 305). In the 460s-470s Marcellinus and his nephew Julius Nepos ruled it as a Roman principality; Nepos, the last western emperor recognised by Constantinople, was murdered near Salona in 480.

provinces.name: Pannonia
provinces.endedNote: divided by Trajan between c. 103 and 107
provinces.capitalName: legate's seat probably Carnuntum (Poetovio and Siscia earlier)

phases.t: Illyricum Inferius, then Pannonia; three legions on the middle Danube; Pannonian mutiny of AD 14

provinces.summary: The middle Danube basin, conquered by Tiberius in 12-9 BC and again in the revolt of 6-9. The mutiny of the Pannonian legions at Tiberius' accession (AD 14), quelled by Drusus with the help of a lunar eclipse, is one of Tacitus' great set pieces. Colonies at Emona, Savaria (Claudius), Siscia and Sirmium (Flavian) Romanised the Amber Road and the Sava valley.

provinces.name: Pannonia Superior
provinces.endedNote: divided by Diocletian into Pannonia I and Savia
provinces.governor: legatus Augusti pro praetore of consular rank

phases.t: three legions; headquarters of Marcus Aurelius in the Marcomannic wars (Meditations, book 2 'at Carnuntum')
Brigetio transferred to Inferior by Caracalla, leaving two legions

provinces.summary: One of the most heavily garrisoned provinces of the empire, facing the Marcomanni and Quadi. Septimius Severus, its governor, was proclaimed emperor at Carnuntum on 9 April 193; the tetrarchs met there in November 308 to settle the succession.
provinces.garrison: X Gemina (Vindobona), XIV Gemina (Carnuntum), I Adiutrix (Brigetio, to 214)

provinces.name: Pannonia Inferior
provinces.endedNote: divided by Diocletian into Pannonia II and Valeria

phases.t: one legion (II Adiutrix at Aquincum); Hadrian governor 107
consular after Caracalla added Brigetio and I Adiutrix

provinces.summary: Facing the Sarmatian Iazyges across the Danube bend, Lower Pannonia was a stepping stone for great careers: Hadrian governed it in 107, and Aquincum was the base for wars against the Iazyges in the 170s. Caracalla moved the boundary in 214 to give it a second legion.

provinces.name: Moesia
provinces.createdNote: formally a province by AD 15 at the latest
provinces.endedNote: split by Domitian in 86
provinces.governor: consular legate (also over Macedonia and Achaea AD 15-44)

phases.t: military command on the lower Danube (Caecina Severus, AD 6)
province; Tiberius' road through the Iron Gates (33/34); Plautius Silvanus Aelianus resettles 100,000 transdanubians (ILS 986)

provinces.summary: The lower Danube command, formalised by AD 15 when Poppaeus Sabinus became legate of Moesia with Macedonia and Achaea, a post he held for 20 years. Its 1st-century history is one of raids across the frozen river by Dacians, Sarmatians and Roxolani. In 85 or 86 the Dacians killed its governor Oppius Sabinus, and Domitian split it.

provinces.name: Moesia Superior
provinces.endedNote: dismembered under Aurelian and Diocletian into Dacia (Aureliana), Moesia I and Dardania
provinces.governor: legatus Augusti pro praetore of consular rank

phases.t: base for Trajan's Dacian wars; Trajan's bridge at Drobeta (Apollodorus, 103-105)
mining district (Dardanian and Kosmaj silver); battle of Naissus against the Goths (268 or 269)

provinces.summary: The middle Danube from Singidunum to the Timok, with the Iron Gates gorge where Trajan's road, carved into the cliff and recorded by the Tabula Traiana, carried his armies to Dacia. Its legionary towns grew into the Balkan cities of late antiquity, and Constantine was born at Naissus.

provinces.name: Moesia Inferior
provinces.endedNote: divided by Diocletian into Moesia II and Scythia
provinces.capitalName: governor's seat disputed (Tomis, Novae or Marcianopolis)
provinces.governor: legatus Augusti pro praetore of consular rank

phases.t: three legions on the lower Danube and the Greek cities of the Pontic coast
two legions after V Macedonica moved to Dacia; Gothic invasions 238-271; Decius killed at Abritus (251)

provinces.summary: The lower Danube and the Dobruja, with the Greek Pentapolis of the Black Sea coast (Tomis, Histria, Callatis, Odessos, Mesembria). Trajan's victory monument at Adamclisi (Tropaeum Traiani, 109) stands here. In the 3rd century it took the full weight of the Gothic invasions, culminating in the death of Decius and his son in the marshes at Abritus in 251.
provinces.garrison: I Italica (Novae), XI Claudia (Durostorum), V Macedonica (Troesmis, to 167)

provinces.name: Dacia
provinces.createdNote: annexed after the second Dacian war, 106
provinces.endedNote: divided by Hadrian c. 119 after the Sarmatian crisis of 117-118

phases.t: Trajan's conquest; colonists brought 'from the whole Roman world' (Eutropius 8.6)

provinces.summary: Conquered in two wars (101-102, 105-106) that ended with Decebalus' suicide, Dacia gave Trajan a gold windfall that paid for his forum. Eutropius says Hadrian thought of giving it up but kept it because so many Roman citizens had been settled there. The gold mines of Alburnus Maior, run by Illyrian miners, left wax tablet contracts dated 131-167.

provinces.name: Dacia Superior / Dacia Apulensis
provinces.endedNote: evacuated under Aurelian (c. 271-275)
provinces.capitalName: Apulum (legionary base); Sarmizegetusa the colonia and seat of the concilium

phases.t: Dacia Superior
renamed Dacia Apulensis within the Tres Daciae

provinces.summary: The core of Roman Transylvania and the Banat, with the gold districts and the colony of Sarmizegetusa, where the council of the Three Dacias met at the altar of the emperor.

provinces.name: Dacia Inferior / Dacia Malvensis
provinces.endedNote: evacuated under Aurelian

phases.t: Dacia Inferior (Oltenia)
Dacia Malvensis within the Tres Daciae

provinces.summary: The Olt valley and Oltenia, guarded by the limes Alutanus and later the limes Transalutanus. A procuratorial province of auxiliary forts and small towns.

provinces.name: Dacia Porolissensis
provinces.endedNote: evacuated under Aurelian

phases.t: carved from Superior in the north of Transylvania
part of the Tres Daciae

provinces.summary: Northern Transylvania with the frontier fortress of Porolissum, a customs post on the Meses gate into barbaricum. Legio V Macedonica came to Potaissa in 168.

provinces.name: Tres Daciae
provinces.endedNote: abandoned by Aurelian, 271 or 274/275 (Eutropius 9.15; Historia Augusta, Aurelian 39.7)
provinces.governor: consular legate over the three Dacian provinces, with procurators under him

phases.t: unified command created during the Marcomannic wars; two legions (XIII Gemina at Apulum, V Macedonica at Potaissa)

provinces.summary: Marcus Aurelius united the three Dacian provinces under one consular legate when the Marcomannic wars threatened them; the first holder, M. Claudius Fronto, died fighting in 170. The province contracted under the 3rd-century invasions, and coin finds thin out after the 250s.

provinces.name: Dacia (Aureliana)
provinces.endedNote: divided (by Diocletian at the latest) into Ripensis and Mediterranea

phases.t: new Dacia carved out of the two Moesias south of the Danube to save face after the evacuation

provinces.summary: When Aurelian withdrew from Trajan's Dacia he created a new 'Dacia' south of the river in the middle of the Moesias, settling the evacuated provincials there. It was soon split into Dacia Ripensis and Dacia Mediterranea.

provinces.name: Thracia
provinces.endedNote: divided under Diocletian into Thracia, Europa, Rhodope and Haemimontus
provinces.governor: equestrian procurator; praetorian legate from Trajan

phases.t: the Odrysian kingdom annexed after the murder of Rhoemetalces III; strategiai retained
praetorian legate; Trajanic city foundations (Augusta Traiana, Traianopolis, Plotinopolis, Nicopolis ad Nestum); Goths sack Philippopolis 250/251

provinces.summary: Rome ran Thrace through Odrysian client kings for almost two centuries before Claudius annexed it in 46. Its 1st-century administration kept the old royal districts; Trajan and Hadrian urbanised it with new cities. Thracians were the empire's great recruiting pool, above all for the praetorian guard and the cavalry.

provinces.name: Judaea / Syria Palaestina
provinces.endedNote: divided c. 390-409 into Palaestina I and II (Salutaris already c. 357-358)
provinces.governor: equestrian prefect (6-41), procurator (44-66); praetorian legate (from 70), consular (from c. 120); praeses (4th c.)

phases.t: prefecture after Archelaus was deposed; census of Quirinius; Pontius Pilate 26-36 (Caesarea inscription)
kingdom of Agrippa I
procurators (Felix, Festus, Florus)
First Jewish Revolt; Jerusalem destroyed 70; Masada 73/74
legate commanding X Fretensis at Jerusalem; second legion and consular rank under Hadrian; Bar Kokhba revolt 132-135
renamed Syria Palaestina; Aelia Capitolina founded on Jerusalem; southern Arabia (Petra, Negev) added under Diocletian

provinces.summary: The province where Roman rule failed most spectacularly. Equestrian governors of a small subprovince of Syria provoked two great revolts; after the second, Hadrian erased the name Judaea, refounded Jerusalem as Aelia Capitolina and barred Jews from it. Under the later empire its rabbinic academies produced the Mishnah (c. 200) and the Jerusalem Talmud.
provinces.garrison: auxiliaries (6-66); X Fretensis (from 70); II Traiana then VI Ferrata at Legio-Caparcotna (from c. 120)

provinces.name: Arabia (Petraea)
provinces.createdNote: annexed in 106 on the death of Rabbel II
provinces.endedNote: Arab conquest, 634-636
provinces.governor: praetorian legate commanding III Cyrenaica; praeses and dux (late); moderator (Justinian, Novel 102, 536)

phases.t: Nabataean kingdom annexed by Cornelius Palma; Via Nova Traiana from Bostra to Aila (111-114)
southern districts (Petra, Negev, Aila) transferred to Palaestina; Arabia extended north into the Hauran
province of the diocese of Oriens; Ghassanid phylarchs (al-Harith, supreme phylarch 529) as allies
Bostra surrendered to Khalid ibn al-Walid (634)

provinces.summary: Trajan annexed Nabataea on the death of king Rabbel II, and the coins say 'Arabia adquisita', not 'capta'. The Babatha archive from the Cave of Letters shows Jewish families going to Roman courts here in the 120s. Philip the Arab came from Shahba in the Hauran and rebuilt it as Philippopolis. In the 6th century the Ghassanid kings guarded its desert frontier for Rome.

provinces.name: Numidia
provinces.createdNote: de facto from 39 (Tac. Hist. 4.48; Dio 59.20.7); a separate province by c. 198
provinces.endedNote: lost in the Arab conquest of the Maghreb (c. 680s-698); Byzantine control in 641 limited to the cities and forts
provinces.governor: legate of III Augusta (praetorian) as governor; consularis (late); praeses under Justinian

phases.t: military district of the legate of III Augusta within Africa Proconsularis (Caligula's reform)
formal province (Severus); Hadrian's address to the army at Lambaesis (128); III Augusta disbanded 238, restored 253
split into Numidia Cirtensis and Numidia Militiana
reunited; Cirta renamed Constantina; Donatist heartland
Vandal and Moorish control (partial Roman recovery 442-455)
Justinianic province; Solomon's campaigns in the Aures (535, 539)

provinces.summary: The army province of Roman Africa, born when Caligula took the legion from the senatorial proconsul in 39. Its legionary fortress at Lambaesis and Trajan's veteran colony of Thamugadi (100) are among the best-preserved Roman sites anywhere; Hadrian's address to the troops there in 128 survives on stone. In late antiquity it was the stronghold of the Donatist church.

provinces.name: Mauretania Caesariensis
provinces.endedNote: status in 641 obscure; only Caesarea and coastal points were held after 534

phases.t: Caligula has Ptolemy of Mauretania killed; revolt of Aedemon
procuratorial province; Moorish wars under Antoninus Pius and in the 250s
province of the diocese of Africa; Sitifensis split off; revolts of Firmus (372-375) and Gildo (397-398)
Vandal, then Moorish kingdoms (Masuna 'king of the Moorish and Roman peoples', 508)
Byzantine hold limited to Caesarea and coastal points (Mauretania II)

provinces.summary: Juba II's capital at Caesarea, a showcase of Hellenistic-Roman culture, became the seat of a procurator when Claudius annexed the kingdom of the murdered Ptolemy. Firmus' revolt of 372-375, put down by Theodosius the Elder, showed how Moorish princes could become Roman generals and rebels at once.

provinces.name: Mauretania Tingitana
provinces.endedNote: overrun by the Vandals from 429
provinces.governor: equestrian procurator; praeses under the diocese of Hispaniae (late)

phases.t: procuratorial; peace treaties with the Baquates recorded on altars at Volubilis (140-280)
southern districts including Volubilis and Sala abandoned
attached to the diocese of Hispaniae; comes Tingitaniae commanding the field units
Vandals cross from Spain (May 429); Septem (Ceuta) later held by Justinian

provinces.summary: Separated from Caesariensis by the Moulouya and wild country, Tingitana looked to Spain, to whose diocese it was attached in the 4th century. Its frontier was managed by treaty: the 'altars of peace' at Volubilis record conferences between procurators and Baquates chiefs. The Vandal crossing of 429 began at its coast.

provinces.name: Armenia (Trajanic)
provinces.endedNote: given up by Hadrian, 117-118
provinces.governor: consular legate (L. Catilius Severus, legate of Cappadocia and Armenia Maior)

phases.t: annexed after the killing of Parthamasiris at Elegeia; abandoned by Hadrian

provinces.summary: Trajan's annexation of Armenia in 114, after he refused to accept the Parthian candidate Parthamasiris, opened his great eastern war. The province lasted only until Hadrian restored a client king in 117-118.

provinces.name: Mesopotamia (Trajanic)
provinces.endedNote: abandoned by Hadrian, 117

phases.t: Trajan's conquest between Euphrates and Tigris

provinces.summary: Eutropius and Festus say Trajan made Armenia, Mesopotamia and Assyria provinces. The Mesopotamian province was swept away by the general revolt of 116-117 and abandoned by Hadrian.

provinces.name: Assyria (Trajanic)
provinces.endedNote: abandoned by Hadrian, 117

phases.t: probably Adiabene beyond the Tigris

provinces.summary: Known only from Eutropius and Festus; most scholars think it meant Adiabene east of the Tigris, and some doubt that it was ever organised.

provinces.name: Mesopotamia
provinces.endedNote: Arab conquest 639-640
provinces.governor: equestrian prefect with two legions (Severan); praeses and dux Mesopotamiae (late)

phases.t: Severan province; Nisibis lost and regained in the 230s-240s and 250s-260s; Galerius' peace of Nisibis (298); Shapur II's three sieges of Nisibis (338, 346, 350)
after Jovian ceded Nisibis and Singara, capital at Amida (sieges of 359, 502-503); Dara built 505-507
Persian conquest under Khosrow II (Dara 604)
restored; conquered by the Arabs under Iyad ibn Ghanm (639-640)

provinces.summary: Severus' new province after his Parthian wars, deliberately governed like Egypt by an equestrian prefect commanding the new I and III Parthica. Cassius Dio thought it a costly mistake that dragged Rome into endless wars, and for four centuries this was the front line with Persia. The fortress of Dara, built by Anastasius to replace lost Nisibis, was the scene of Belisarius' victory in 530.
provinces.garrison: I Parthica (Singara), III Parthica (Rhesaena?); late: legions at Amida, Constantia, Cefa

provinces.name: Osrhoene
provinces.endedNote: Arab conquest 638-639

phases.t: most of the kingdom annexed by Severus; Abgar VIII left in Edessa as client
Caracalla deposes Abgar IX; Caracalla murdered near Carrhae (217)
Abgar X restored by Gordian III
Roman province; Edessa a centre of Syriac Christianity; Persian sieges (544)
Persian occupation
restored; Edessa surrendered to Iyad ibn Ghanm (638/639)

provinces.summary: The kingdom of the Abgarids of Edessa, absorbed in stages between 195 and 242. Edessa became the cradle of Syriac literature and of the legend of king Abgar's letter from Christ and his miraculous portrait; Procopius says the city believed it could never be taken, and in 544 Khosrow I failed to take it.

provinces.name: Syria Coele
provinces.endedNote: reorganised under Diocletian; Augusta Euphratensis separated
provinces.capitalName: Antiochia (briefly subordinated to Laodicea as punishment)

phases.t: northern Syria with two legions; Shapur I sacks Antioch (253 or 256)

provinces.summary: The northern half of Severus' divided Syria, keeping Antioch and two legions (IV Scythica at Zeugma, XVI Flavia Firma at Sura). Severus punished Antioch for backing Niger by making Laodicea the metropolis for a time.

provinces.name: Syria Phoenice
provinces.endedNote: divided under Diocletian into Phoenice and Augusta Libanensis

phases.t: southern Syria with Tyre, Emesa, Damascus and Palmyra; legio III Gallica at Raphanea

provinces.summary: Severus' southern Syrian province. Its legion, III Gallica at Raphanea, proclaimed the 14-year-old Elagabalus emperor in 218 at the instigation of his grandmother Julia Maesa of the priestly family of Emesa. Palmyra lay within it until Odaenathus and Zenobia turned the city into an empire.

provinces.name: Hispania Nova Citerior Antoniniana
provinces.endedNote: reabsorbed into Tarraconensis, probably by c. 235-238

phases.t: northwestern Spain separated from Tarraconensis by Caracalla

provinces.summary: A short-lived province known from inscriptions of its first legate, C. Iulius Cerealis, carved out of the northwest of Tarraconensis around the mining districts and legio VII Gemina. It was reabsorbed within a generation; Diocletian's Gallaecia revived the idea.

provinces.name: Caria et Phrygia
provinces.endedNote: divided under Diocletian into Caria and Phrygia I-II

phases.t: carved out of Asia in the mid-3rd century

provinces.summary: A province separated from Asia around 250, known chiefly from inscriptions at Aphrodisias, which became its capital and thereby joined the rank of governors' seats. It was the forerunner of Diocletian's further subdivision of Asia.

provinces.name: Syria (Coele), later Syria Prima
provinces.createdNote: Diocletianic Syria (Coele), attested in the Verona List
provinces.endedNote: Arab conquest 636-637
provinces.governor: consularis (Notitia); the comes Orientis resided at Antioch

phases.t: Syria (Coele) of the diocese of Oriens; Julian's quarrel with Antioch (Misopogon, 363); Riot of the Statues (387)
Syria Prima after Syria Salutaris was separated; earthquake and fire of May 526
Theodorias carved from its coast (528); Khosrow I sacks Antioch (540) and deports its people to Veh-Antiok-Khosrow
Persian occupation
restored; Antioch surrendered to the Arabs after the Yarmuk

provinces.summary: Antioch was the third city of the empire and seat of the comes Orientis and the magister militum per Orientem, so its governor was overshadowed by great men. The Riot of the Statues in 387 produced John Chrysostom's homilies; the earthquake of 526, said by Malalas to have killed 250,000, and Khosrow's sack of 540 broke the city. The limestone massif to the east, with Simeon the Stylite's pillar at Telanissos, preserves hundreds of late Roman olive-growing villages.

provinces.name: Syria Salutaris (Syria Secunda)
provinces.createdNote: by c. 400 (listed in the Notitia Dignitatum); often dated c. 415
provinces.endedNote: Arab conquest 636-637

phases.t: province of the Orontes valley: Apamea, Epiphania, Larissa, Arethusa, Raphanea
Khosrow I at Apamea (540); sacked by the Persian general Adarmahan (573)
Persian occupation
restored; Arab conquest

provinces.summary: The middle Orontes, centred on Apamea, the Seleucid cavalry depot and later a centre of Neoplatonism. Procopius tells how in 540 bishop Thomas paraded the city's relic of the True Cross, which flamed without burning, and Khosrow contented himself with plunder. The Persian sack of 573 carried off much of its population.

provinces.name: Theodorias
provinces.endedNote: Arab conquest 637-638

phases.t: created by Justinian from the coast of Syria I and named for Theodora
Persian occupation
restored; Arab conquest of the coast

provinces.summary: A small coastal province named for the empress Theodora, created in 528 out of Laodicea, Gabala, Paltos and Balaneae, partly as relief after the earthquakes of 526 and 528 at Antioch. It is a good example of Justinian's habit of naming cities and provinces after himself and his wife.

provinces.name: Augusta Euphratensis
provinces.endedNote: Arab conquest 637-638

phases.t: Commagene and Cyrrhestice: Samosata, Zeugma, Cyrrhus, Germanicia, Sergiopolis
Hierapolis ransoms itself from Khosrow I (540); Sergiopolis a Ghassanid and imperial pilgrimage centre
Persian occupation
restored; Hierapolis surrendered to the Arabs (637)

provinces.summary: The Euphrates crossings of north Syria, including old Commagene (Lucian came from Samosata). Theodoret, bishop of Cyrrhus 423-c. 457, describes its holy men in his Religious History. Sergiopolis (Resafa) in the steppe, with the shrine of St Sergius, drew gifts from Justinian and from Khosrow II alike and was the meeting place of the Ghassanid confederation.

provinces.name: Phoenice
provinces.createdNote: Diocletianic; listed in the Verona List
provinces.endedNote: Arab conquest 635-637

phases.t: coastal Phoenicia: Tyre, Sidon, Berytus, Byblos, Tripolis, Paneas
Berytus wrecked by the earthquake and tsunami of 9 July 551, ending its law school
Persian occupation
restored; Arab conquest

provinces.summary: The Phoenician coast, famous for Tyrian purple, silk weaving and the law school of Berytus, where future lawyers of the eastern empire studied for five years; two of Justinian's Digest commissioners, Dorotheus and Anatolius, taught there. The 551 earthquake destroyed Berytus and the school moved to Sidon.

provinces.name: Augusta Libanensis / Phoenice Libanensis
provinces.createdNote: Verona List (Augusta Libanensis); Phoenice Libanensis in the Notitia
provinces.endedNote: Arab conquest 635-636

phases.t: the inland province: Emesa, Damascus, Heliopolis, Palmyra (Diocletian's camp with legio I Illyricorum)
Persian occupation
restored; Damascus fell in September 635, Emesa in 636

provinces.summary: Inland Syria behind Lebanon, including the desert frontier of the Strata Diocletiana, whose road and forts ran from Palmyra to Damascus. Heliopolis (Baalbek) kept its great pagan sanctuary until Theodosius I. The Verona List calls it Augusta Libanensis; it may have been abolished and recreated before c. 400.

provinces.name: Palaestina Prima
provinces.createdNote: created c. 390-400 when Palaestina was divided (tres Palaestinae attested 409)
provinces.endedNote: Arab conquest 634-640/641

phases.t: Judaea, Samaria and the coast with Jerusalem and Gaza; Samaritan revolts (484, 529-530)
proconsul of Palaestina (Novel 103), with authority over the troops in emergencies; Samaritan revolt of 556
Persian conquest; Jerusalem sacked in May 614 and the True Cross taken to Ctesiphon
restored; Heraclius returned the Cross to Jerusalem (March 630); Arab conquest (Ajnadayn 634, Jerusalem 637/638, Caesarea 640/641)

provinces.summary: The Holy Land of the Christian empire: Constantine's Church of the Holy Sepulchre (dedicated 335), the empress Eudocia's residence in Jerusalem, a patriarchate from 451, and the rhetorical school of Gaza. Its Samaritan revolts were crushed with great slaughter, and Justinian's Novel 103 gave its governor proconsular rank in response. Jerusalem's surrender to Umar was negotiated by the patriarch Sophronius.

provinces.name: Palaestina Secunda
provinces.endedNote: Arab conquest 635-636

phases.t: Galilee, the Golan and the western Decapolis; the Jewish patriarchate at Tiberias until c. 425
Persian occupation
restored; Arab victories at Pella/Fahl (635) and the Yarmuk (636)

provinces.summary: The north of Palestine, with Scythopolis and the lake of Tiberias, where the Jerusalem Talmud was completed and the patriarchs of the Jewish community sat until the office lapsed c. 425. The decisive Arab victory on the Yarmuk (August 636) was fought on its eastern edge.

provinces.name: Palaestina Salutaris (Tertia)
provinces.createdNote: c. 357-358, from parts of Arabia and Palaestina
provinces.governor: praeses; dux Palaestinae commanded the troops

phases.t: Palaestina Salutaris: the Negev, southern Transjordan, Sinai, Aila (legio X Fretensis)
renamed Palaestina Tertia; Justinian's fortified monastery on Sinai (548-565)
Aila submitted to Muhammad at Tabuk (630); the rest lost by 636

provinces.summary: The desert south: the Negev towns of Elusa, Nessana and Shivta (whose papyri record taxes, camels and soldiers' pay), Petra, whose carbonised 6th-century papyri were found in 1993, and Sinai, where Justinian built the walled monastery now called St Catherine's. Aila on the Red Sea was the first Roman town to make terms with Muhammad, in 630.

provinces.name: Cilicia (Prima)
provinces.endedNote: still Roman in 641; lost to the Arabs in the later 7th century

phases.t: Cilicia of the diocese of Oriens; Julian buried at Tarsus (363)
Cilicia Prima after the creation of Cilicia II; Justinian's flood works on the Cydnus at Tarsus
Persian occupation (Tarsus taken 613)
restored; became the Arab-Byzantine frontier zone after 641

provinces.summary: The western Cilician plain with Tarsus, Adana and Pompeiopolis. Julian was buried outside Tarsus after his Persian campaign. In the decades after 641 Cilicia became a no-man's-land between the caliphate and Byzantium.

provinces.name: Cilicia Secunda
provinces.endedNote: still Roman in 641

phases.t: eastern Cilicia: Anazarbus, Mopsuestia, Aegeae, Epiphania; Anazarbus rebuilt after earthquakes and renamed after Justin I
Persian occupation
restored

provinces.summary: Eastern Cilicia, with Anazarbus and Mopsuestia, home of Theodore of Mopsuestia, whose writings Justinian had condemned in the Three Chapters controversy (553).

provinces.name: Isauria
provinces.endedNote: still Roman in 641
provinces.governor: praeses with a comes rei militaris; praetor combining civil and military power (Novel 27, 535)

phases.t: Rough Cilicia and the Isaurian highlands, including Lycaonia
Lycaonia separated; Isaurian raids (353-354, 404-408); Zeno emperor 474-491; Isaurian war 492-497
praetor Iustinianus

provinces.summary: Rome never fully tamed the Isaurian highlanders, who raided their neighbours and terrorised Asia Minor in 404-408. Their chieftains became imperial generals: one of them, Tarasicodissa, renamed himself Zeno and became emperor (474-491). Anastasius fought a five-year war (492-497) to break their power and deported many to Thrace.

provinces.name: Aegyptus Iovia / Aegyptus (later I and II)
provinces.endedNote: Arab conquest; last Roman troops left Alexandria in September 642
provinces.governor: praeses, then governed directly by the praefectus Augustalis; dux et augustalis (Edict 13, c. 539)

phases.t: Aegyptus Iovia (western Delta and Alexandria)
Aegyptus; Alexandrian riots, Serapeum destroyed (391/392), Hypatia killed (415); later divided into Aegyptus I and II
Justinian's Edict 13 fuses civil and military command in each Egyptian unit
Persian occupation
restored; Arab conquest (Babylon April 641, treaty of Alexandria November 641, evacuation September 642)

provinces.summary: Alexandria and the western Delta. The province's governor counted for little beside the Augustal prefect and the patriarch, the most powerful bishop of the East, who could fill the streets with monks. Edict 13 fixed the grain tax shipped to Constantinople at 8 million artabae a year. The patriarch Cyrus negotiated the surrender of Alexandria to Amr ibn al-As.

provinces.name: Aegyptus Herculia / Augustamnica
provinces.createdNote: Herculia in the Verona List; renamed Augustamnica c. 341
provinces.endedNote: Arab conquest 640-641

phases.t: Aegyptus Herculia (eastern Delta and Heptanomia)
Augustamnica; divided into Augustamnica I (Pelusium) and II in the 5th century
Persian occupation
restored; Pelusium taken by Amr ibn al-As after a siege (early 640)

provinces.summary: The eastern Delta and the Sinai coast, guarding the land route from Syria. Pelusium was the door of Egypt: the Persian invasion of 618-619 and Amr's of 639-640 both came that way, and the plague of 541 first appeared there.

provinces.name: Arcadia
provinces.endedNote: Arab conquest 641

phases.t: Middle Egypt (Heptanomia) including the Fayum, named for the emperor Arcadius
Persian occupation
restored; Arab conquest

provinces.summary: Middle Egypt, named after Arcadius. Oxyrhynchus has given us more papyri than any other site, from lost Greek literature to the accounts of the great Apion family, whose estates in the 6th century employed thousands and maintained their own postal service, bath-heating and police.
scholarship: Sarris, Economy and Society in the Age of Justinian (2006)

provinces.name: Thebais
provinces.endedNote: Arab conquest 641
provinces.capitalName: Antinoopolis (Ptolemais Hermiou in the Upper Thebaid)
provinces.governor: praeses; dux Thebaidos; under Justinian a dux et augustalis

phases.t: Upper Egypt; Diocletian withdraws the frontier from the Dodecaschoenus to Philae (298)
divided into Lower and Upper Thebaid; Narses closes the temples of Philae (c. 535-537)
Persian occupation
restored; Arab conquest

provinces.summary: Upper Egypt, the land of Pachomian monasticism and of Shenoute's White Monastery. Diocletian pulled the frontier back to Philae and paid the Nobatae and Blemmyes subsidies; Philae's Isis temple, the last functioning pagan temple of the empire, was closed under Justinian. The 6th-century archive of Dioscorus of Aphrodito, notary and poet, shows village life under its dukes.

provinces.name: Libya Superior (Pentapolis)
provinces.endedNote: Arab conquest 642-643

phases.t: Cyrenaica (Pentapolis); capital moved from Cyrene to Ptolemais
raids of the Austuriani (405-412); Justinian's fortifications
Persian occupation
restored; Amr ibn al-As takes Barca (642/643)

provinces.summary: Cyrenaica in decline: the letters of Synesius, philosopher-bishop of Ptolemais (c. 410-413), describe how he organised the defence of his city against desert raiders when the imperial troops failed. Cyrene itself never recovered from the revolt of 115-117 and the earthquake of 365.

provinces.name: Libya Inferior (Libya Sicca, Marmarica)
provinces.endedNote: Arab conquest 642

phases.t: the desert coast between the Delta and Cyrenaica

provinces.summary: The dry coast west of Alexandria, with the port of Paraetonium and the desert road to the oracle of Ammon at Siwa. A poor province of nomads and small garrisons.

provinces.name: Bithynia
provinces.endedNote: still Roman in 641

phases.t: Diocletian's capital at Nicomedia; Great Persecution begins there (23-24 February 303); Council of Nicaea (325); earthquake of 358
reduced by the creation of Honorias; Council of Chalcedon (451)

provinces.summary: The hinterland of Constantinople. Nicomedia was Diocletian's capital, where his palace overlooked the church he had demolished to start the Great Persecution; Constantine died nearby in 337. Two ecumenical councils met in the province, at Nicaea in 325 and Chalcedon in 451.

provinces.name: Honorias
provinces.endedNote: merged with Paphlagonia by Novel 29 (535)

phases.t: created from eastern Bithynia and western Paphlagonia under Theodosius I, named for Honorius

provinces.summary: A small province between Bithynia and Paphlagonia, with Claudiopolis (birthplace of Hadrian's favourite Antinous as Bithynium), Heraclea Pontica, Tium and Prusias ad Hypium. Justinian merged it with Paphlagonia in 535 as a cost-saving measure.

provinces.name: Paphlagonia
provinces.endedNote: still Roman in 641
provinces.governor: corrector (Notitia); praetor of Paphlagonia and Honorias (Novel 29, 535)

phases.t: Diocletianic province; Council of Gangra (c. 340) condemns extreme asceticism
merged with Honorias under a praetor

provinces.summary: A rugged land of horse-breeding and small cities on the Black Sea coast. The Council of Gangra condemned the followers of Eustathius of Sebasteia for denouncing marriage and encouraging slaves to leave their masters.

provinces.name: Galatia (Prima)
provinces.endedNote: still Roman in 641

phases.t: reduced Galatia; Council of Ancyra (314); Julian at Ancyra (362)
Galatia Prima after Galatia Salutaris was separated
Persian raid on Ancyra (c. 620-622)

provinces.summary: The Celtic heartland round Ancyra, now an important road junction between Constantinople and the eastern frontier. Its council of 314 is one of the earliest sources of canon law on the lapsed.

provinces.name: Galatia Salutaris (Secunda)
provinces.endedNote: still Roman in 641

phases.t: western Galatia, separated under Theodosius I

provinces.summary: Western Galatia with Pessinus, whose sacred stone of the Mother of the Gods was brought to Rome in 204 BC; Julian worshipped there on his way east in 362 and found the cult nearly deserted.

provinces.name: Cappadocia (Prima)
provinces.endedNote: still Roman in 641

phases.t: reduced Cappadocia; huge imperial estates (domus divina)
Cappadocia Prima after Valens' division
proconsul with authority over the agents of the imperial estates (Novel 30); Persians hold Caesarea 611-612

provinces.summary: The land of the Cappadocian Fathers, with Basil as bishop of Caesarea (370-379) building his hospital complex, the Basileias. Its imperial horse-studs and crown estates were so extensive that Justinian complained their managers terrorised the province, and gave its governor proconsular rank to control them.

provinces.name: Cappadocia Secunda
provinces.endedNote: still Roman in 641

phases.t: created by Valens from southwestern Cappadocia

provinces.summary: Valens' division of Cappadocia in 371/372 made Tyana a provincial capital and its bishop Anthimus a metropolitan, provoking Basil to create new sees, including the wretched post-station of Sasima, where he consecrated his friend Gregory of Nazianzus. The province controlled the road to the Cilician Gates.

provinces.name: Diospontus / Helenopontus
provinces.endedNote: still Roman in 641

phases.t: Diospontus (Verona List)
renamed Helenopontus after Constantine's mother
moderator, with cities of Pontus Polemoniacus added (Novel 28)

provinces.summary: The western Pontus with Amaseia (birthplace of Strabo), Amisus and Sinope, home of Diogenes the Cynic and of the heretic Marcion. Constantine renamed it for his mother Helena, whose birthplace Drepanum in Bithynia had already become Helenopolis.

provinces.name: Pontus Polemoniacus
provinces.endedNote: divided by Novels 28 and 31 (535-536)

phases.t: the kingdom of Polemon II annexed by Nero (64), attached to Galatia then Cappadocia
separate province (Verona List) with Neocaesarea, Comana Pontica, Polemonium, Cerasus and Trapezus

provinces.summary: The eastern Pontic coast and its hinterland. Trapezus was the base of legio I Pontica and the Pontic fleet. Gregory the Wonderworker, bishop of Neocaesarea in the 3rd century, was credited with converting the region. Justinian divided it between Helenopontus and the new Armenia I.

provinces.name: Armenia (Minor)
provinces.endedNote: divided c. 386

phases.t: Lesser Armenia and Melitene, formerly districts of Cappadocia

provinces.summary: Lesser Armenia west of the upper Euphrates, a client kingdom until 72 and thereafter part of Cappadocia, made a province by Diocletian. Its legionary bases at Satala and Melitene anchored the northern frontier with Persia. It was divided into Armenia I and II under Theodosius I.

provinces.name: Armenia Prima (Armenia Secunda from 536)
provinces.endedNote: still Roman in 641

phases.t: Armenia Prima: Sebasteia, Nicopolis, Satala (legio XV Apollinaris), Colonia
renumbered Armenia Secunda by Novel 31, losing Satala and Nicopolis to the new Armenia I

provinces.summary: Sebasteia, scene of the martyrdom of the Forty Martyrs on a frozen lake (c. 320) and seat of the ascetic bishop Eustathius, was its capital. Satala's legion guarded the route into Armenia proper.

provinces.name: Armenia Secunda (Armenia Tertia from 536)
provinces.endedNote: still Roman in 641

phases.t: Armenia Secunda: Melitene (legio XII Fulminata), Arca, Arabissus, Cucusus, Comana
renumbered Armenia Tertia under a comes (Novel 31); Roman victory over Khosrow I near Melitene (576)

provinces.summary: The Melitene district, base of XII Fulminata since Vespasian. John Chrysostom spent his exile (404-407) in the mountain village of Cucusus here. In 576 Khosrow I, retreating after burning Melitene, was defeated nearby by the general Justinian, one of the few Roman victories over a Persian king in person.

provinces.name: Armenia Interior (Roman Armenia)
provinces.endedNote: became the core of Armenia I (Novel 31, 536)
provinces.governor: Arsacid king until c. 390; then comes Armeniae; magister militum per Armeniam from 528

phases.t: Roman share of the partition of Armenia (c. 387); Theodosiopolis fortified under Theodosius II
Justinian creates the magister militum per Armeniam (Sittas)

provinces.summary: When Theodosius I and Shapur III partitioned Armenia around 387, Rome took the smaller western share, first under an Arsacid king and then under a count. Theodosiopolis (Erzurum) became the key fortress facing Persarmenia. Justinian folded it into his new Armenia I in 536.

provinces.name: Armenia Prima (Justinianic)
provinces.endedNote: still Roman in 641

phases.t: Armenia Interior with Theodosiopolis, Satala, Nicopolis, Colonia, Trapezus and Cerasus
enlarged after Maurice's peace with Khosrow II (591) brought most of Persarmenia under Rome; Arab raids from 640 (Dvin sacked October 640)

provinces.summary: Justinian's reorganisation of 536 created four Armenian provinces in place of the old military district, putting Roman Armenia under normal civil government for the first time. Its proconsul's province reached from the Black Sea at Trapezus to Theodosiopolis.

provinces.name: Armenia Quarta
provinces.endedNote: still Roman in 641

phases.t: the Armenian satrapies (Sophene, Anzitene, Ingilene, Asthianene, Balabitene), whose hereditary satraps lost their privileges after backing Illus' revolt (484)
