The series continues with Apollo/horse (ROMANO), Hercules/she-wolf and twins (ROMANO, RRC 20, c. 269-266), Mars/horse head (ROMA), Roma/Victory, and ends with the quadrigatus (Janus/Jupiter in quadriga with Victory, ROMA incuse on a tablet, RRC 28-34) struck in very large numbers c. 225-212 to pay for the Gallic and Hannibalic wars and debased during the crisis. Associated bronze and the Janus/oath-scene gold staters and half-staters (RRC 28-29, c. 216) belong to the same system. Identification: the earliest pieces read ROMANO, later ROMA; all are didrachms or fractions on the Campanian standard, never denarii; the quadrigatus can be hard to tell from imitations struck by allies. Mint location is still argued: Neapolis, Capua, Rome itself, or several mints.

mints.name: Luceria (Lucera), auxiliary mint of the Second Punic War
mints.notes: One of several mints that Rome operated outside the city during the Hannibalic war. Coins with the monogram or letter L (Crawford RRC 97-99) are assigned to the Latin colony of Luceria in Apulia, close to the main Roman armies facing Hannibal. Output includes early denarii, quinarii and sestertii, victoriati and bronze on the reduced sextantal standard. Pieces of the 'L' series are among those that tie the denarius to c. 211: their associated bronze sits at the sextantal stage. Similar regional series carry other symbols (a corn-ear for Sicily, KA, CA, MA and monograms whose attribution remains open).

mints.name: Sicilian mint of the corn-ear series
mints.notes: Coins with a corn-ear (Crawford's 'corn-ear' group, including the gold 60/40/20 as pieces marked with value numerals and early denarii and victoriati) are attributed to a Roman mint operating in Sicily during and after the siege of Syracuse (213-211). The corn-ear points to Sicilian grain. The group matters for dating: excavations at Morgantina, sacked by the Romans in 211, found early denarii and associated issues sealed in the destruction levels, the strongest archaeological evidence for Crawford's c. 211 date for the introduction of the denarius against the older 187 or 269 dates.

mints.name: Corfinium renamed Italia (Social War rebel mint)
mints.notes: The confederated Italians made Corfinium their capital, renamed it Italia, and struck denarii on the Roman standard, consciously answering Roman types. Obverses show the head of Italia (laureate or helmeted); reverses include an oath scene with warriors touching a sow with their swords, the Italian bull goring the Roman wolf, Dioscuri and a warrior with a bull. Legends are Latin (ITALIA) or Oscan (VITELIU, the name of the commanders Q. Poppaedius Silo and C. Papius Mutilus in Oscan script). As the war turned, production shifted to Bovianum and Aesernia. Many issues are overstruck on Roman denarii, which shows where the silver came from. All are rare and heavily faked; genuine pieces have the flat, shallow relief and slightly irregular flans of the Roman denarius of the 90s, and die studies (Campana) list most known dies.

mints.name: Paestum (last civic mint of Italy)
mints.notes: The Latin colony of 273 BC kept the right to strike small bronze long after every other Italian community had stopped. Its semisses and quadrantes of the late Republic and early Principate carry PS S C (Paestum, by decree of the local senate) and the names of local magistrates; a few issues name Tiberius, and the series ends under him. Collectors meet them as small, crude, heavily patinated bronzes with Bona Mens, a cornucopia or a temple. They are the last flicker of the civic coinages of Italy, which the Roman state otherwise absorbed by the end of the Social War.

mints.name: Bolskan / Osca (Huesca): Iberian denarius mint
mints.notes: The most prolific of the Iberian denarius mints of the Ebro valley. Bolskan denarii (bearded male head right / horseman with lance) were struck on the Roman weight standard from the mid-2nd century, apparently to pay native levies and taxes in Roman service, and production peaked in the 80s-70s when Osca was Sertorius' capital (Plutarch, Sertorius 14, his school for noble Iberian boys). Their mass in Spanish hoards that close in the 70s is a principal witness to the cost of the Sertorian war. Many other Iberian mints (Turiasu, Sekobirikes, Arekorata, Ikalesken) struck the same types; identification depends on reading the Iberian legend under the horseman. Common, but beware cast copies.

mints.name: Massalia (Marseille)
mints.notes: Rome's oldest overseas friend struck silver from the late 6th century: drachms (Artemis / lion) on a light standard close to the Roman victoriatus, abundant obols (Apollo / wheel with MA), and bronze (Apollo / bull). Massaliot drachms were widely imitated in the Po valley and the Alps, where 'Padane drachms' with corrupt lion types formed a separate currency. Caesar's siege of 49 BC and the city's capitulation ended its political independence and, on the usual view, its silver coinage. Identification: obols are tiny (c. 0.6-0.7 g) with a four-spoked wheel; the Celtic imitations have stylised, often unreadable legends.

mints.name: Utica: Pompeian military mint in Africa
mints.notes: After Pharsalus the Pompeian leadership regrouped in Africa and struck denarii and some gold at a mint usually placed at Utica, where Cato commanded. Types: Metellus Scipio's elephant (an allusion to his family's victory at Panormus in 250 BC) and the African genius with lion skin; Cato's Roma seated / VICTRIX; Eppius' Hercules. Juba I of Numidia struck his own denarii (bearded king / temple, REX IVBA in Latin and Neo-Punic) at an uncertain royal mint, on the same standard, showing how closely the war finance was shared. The Thapsus campaign (46) ended the series. Rare to scarce; Scipio's elephant denarius is the common one.

mints.name: Emerita Augusta (Mérida)
mints.notes: Founded in 25 BC by Augustus' legate P. Carisius for veterans of the Cantabrian war (V Alaudae and X Gemina). Carisius struck denarii, quinarii and some aurei: the bare head of Augustus with IMP CAESAR AVGVST and reverses of captured Cantabrian weapons (helmet, double axe, sword, round shield), a trophy and the city gate with EMERITA over the arch, one of the earliest city views on Roman coins. Thereafter the colony struck bronze under Augustus, Tiberius and Caligula (priest ploughing the pomerium, city gate, Divus Augustus with altar). Carisius' denarii are scarce and prized for the gate type; check the gate's two arches and the inscription spacing against published dies.

mints.name: Colonia Patricia (Córdoba), Augustan 'Spanish' mint
mints.notes: RIC I² assigns a large Augustan gold and silver coinage of c. 19-16 BC, struck in the aftermath of the Cantabrian wars and the Parthian settlement, to Colonia Patricia, with other groups to an uncertain second Spanish mint (often thought to be Caesaraugusta or Emerita). Types: the oak-wreathed head of Augustus (CAESAR AVGVSTVS), SIGNIS RECEPTIS with standards and the clipeus virtutis (CL V), the Parthian kneeling with a standard, the round temple of Mars Ultor holding the recovered standards, the comet of Divus Iulius, OB CIVIS SERVATOS. Without mint marks, attribution rests on style (fuller portraits than Rome's) and hoard distribution, and the location has been argued for a century. These are the commonest Augustan denarii after the Gaius-Lucius type of Lugdunum.

mints.name: Caesaraugusta (Zaragoza), colonial mint
mints.notes: Veteran colony of veterans from IV Macedonica, VI Victrix and X Gemina, whose numbers appear on its bronzes with vexilla and aquila. The founding type shows the priest ploughing the sacred furrow with a yoke of oxen. Names of local duoviri date issues; series run from Augustus to Caligula, when Spanish civic coinage ends (traditionally linked to Caligula's displeasure, though the mechanism is unknown). Large, well-made asses and dupondii of Tiberius (with Augustus as DIVVS) and Caligula's issues for Agrippina and Germanicus are popular with collectors.

mints.name: Tarraco (Tarragona)
mints.notes: The colony (Colonia Victrix Togata Tarraco or Iulia Urbs Triumphalis) struck bronze under Augustus and Tiberius, notably the altar with a palm sprouting from it, the omen reported to Augustus and answered with his famous joke that this showed how often they sacrificed (Quintilian 6.3.77). In 68 Galba, proclaimed in Spain, struck aurei and denarii there and at other Spanish mints (HISPANIA, SALVS GEN HVMANI, Roma and Victory types, and the 'autonomous' civil-war denarii without portraits). Vespasian's earliest western gold and silver (69-70) is also attributed to Tarraco by RIC II²; it is usually recognised by a tiny globe at the point of the bust and by distinctive lettering.

mints.name: Colonia Nemausus (Nîmes)
mints.notes: Struck the most recognisable colonial bronze of the West: back-to-back heads of Agrippa (with rostral crown) and Augustus, IMP DIVI F, and reverse a crocodile chained to a palm tree with COL NEM, celebrating the conquest of Egypt and the settlement of veterans of the Egyptian campaign. Three main series (c. 28 BC, c. 16-10 BC, c. AD 10-14) can be separated by Augustus' laurel wreath and the P P (pater patriae, after 2 BC) on the last. Specimens are very often cut in half, because they circulated as small change across Gaul and on the Rhine; a rare variant has a leg-shaped flange ('pied de sanglier'), probably a votive form. Large numbers turn up in German military sites before AD 9.

mints.name: Lugdunum (Lyon)
marks: (none, 15 BC-AD 69; globe at bust point on Nero's aes)
mints.officinae: 3 under the Tetrarchy and Constantine (P, S, T); 2 in the later 4th c.
mints.notes: Augustus made the capital of the Three Gauls his main gold and silver mint around 15 BC (Strabo 4.3.2 notes gold and silver struck there). It produced the Gaius and Lucius Caesares denarius (2 BC-AD 4, the commonest Augustan denarius) and Tiberius' 'tribute penny' (PONTIF MAXIM, seated female often identified as Livia), plus the great 'Altar of Lugdunum' series of asses, semisses and sesterces with the Altar of Rome and Augustus (ROM ET AVG), dedicated 12/10 BC. Precious-metal production returned to Rome under Caligula. Nero reopened it for aes in 64-67: Lugdunum Neronian sestertii and asses are identified by a small globe at the point of the bust. Galba, Vitellius and Vespasian struck aes here; Clodius Albinus struck his own denarii and aurei in 195-197. Aurelian reopened the mint in 274 with personnel from the closed Gallic mint at Cologne. In the 4th c. look for PLG/SLG, later LVGD, LVGP, LVGS, with crescents, stars and pellets; gold with LVGOB is rare. It ended with the usurpers of 407-413.

mints.name: Colonia Agrippina (Cologne), Gallic Empire mint
mints.notes: The usurpation of Postumus in 260 created a separate western coinage that lasted until Tetricus' surrender in 274. Two mints are distinguished by style and hoard evidence ('Mint I' and 'Mint II'): older literature put them at Lyon and Cologne, more recent work at Trier and Cologne, and the identifications are still argued. Postumus' early antoniniani were noticeably better than Gallienus' (c. 15-20% silver) and his gold is among the finest of the century, with superb facing portraits and Hercules labours. The fineness collapsed under Victorinus and the Tetrici to a few per cent. Cologne's coins are recognised by a distinctive Postumus portrait and by reverse groups such as SAECVLI FELICITAS; Laelianus and Marius are associated with Mainz/Cologne style. When Aurelian reunified the empire the staff went to Lugdunum.

mints.name: Treveri (Trier)
mints.officinae: 2 (P, S) normally; A and B under the Tetrarchy.
mints.notes: Probably already a Gallic Empire mint, Trier became a regular imperial mint when Constantius I made it his capital in 293/4. It was the main western gold mint of the 4th century: the Beaurains (Arras) treasure contains Trier solidi and multiples, and Trier struck enormous numbers of nummi for Constantine's GLORIA EXERCITVS, VRBS ROMA and CONSTANTINOPOLIS types (330-335) and for Constantine II. Marks: PTR/STR (officina first) and TRP/TRS (officina last), with crescents, dots and wreaths that identify sub-issues; precious-metal marks TROB (gold, OB = obryzum, refined) and TRPS (silver, PS = pusulatum) from c. 367. Magnentius and Decentius struck here in quantity (big CHI-RHO 'Salus' bronzes, 353), as did Magnus Maximus and Flavius Victor (383-388). After the praetorian prefecture moved to Arles c. 395-407, Trier struck only for Constantine III (407-411) and Jovinus (411-413).

mints.name: Londinium (London), later Augusta
mints.notes: Opened by Carausius (286/7-293) and continued by Allectus (293-296), who marked coins L or ML (moneta Londiniensis) and, after an attempt to align with the central coinage, ML XXI. The enigmatic silver denarii and gold of Carausius with RSR in the exergue (expanded as Redeunt Saturnia Regna, from Virgil Eclogue 4.6, a reading backed by the INPCDA medallion) belong to the start of the revolt; their mint is uncertain. After Constantius I recovered Britain in 296 London struck unmarked folles, then LON, and under Constantine PLN, PLON, MLL and MLN (marks on which numismatists still argue), with the SOLI INVICTO COMITI, BEATA TRANQVILLITAS (VOTIS XX altar) and VIRTVS EXERCIT types. Closed c. 325. Magnus Maximus revived it under the city's new name Augusta: AVGOB solidi and AVGPS siliquae of Maximus are great rarities, almost the only 'London' coins after 325. Identification: Carausian radiates with S P or S C in the field and ML/L in the exergue; 'C' marks belong to the second Carausian mint.

mints.name: 'C' mint of Carausius and Allectus (Camulodunum?)
mints.notes: The second British mint of the usurpers, marked C. Camulodunum (Colchester) is the traditional identification; Clausentum (Bitterne), Glevum (Gloucester) and a mint travelling with the court have also been proposed, and QC has even been read Quinarius Camuloduni or Clausentensis. C-mint radiates tend to be cruder than London's and carry more unusual reverse types (PAX with vertical sceptre is common to both). Allectus' C-mint quinarii with a galley (VIRTVS AVG, QC) are a characteristic denomination: a small radiate weighing about half the normal coin, whose real function is debated.

mints.name: Ambianum (Amiens)
mints.notes: Opened by Magnentius, who was born at Amiens according to tradition, during his usurpation. It struck the standard Magnentian bronze types (VICTORIAE DD NN AVG ET CAES, two Victories holding a wreath inscribed VOT V MVLT X, and the great chi-rho with alpha and omega, SALVS DD NN AVG ET CAES) for Magnentius and his Caesar Decentius, plus rare gold. It closed after Constantius II's victory. The short life and single dynasty make Amiens pieces scarce and sought after; the AMB mark is unambiguous.

mints.name: Arelate (Arles), renamed Constantina
mints.notes: Constantine transferred the staff of Maxentius' Ostia mint to Arles in 313. Early marks are ARL with officina letters, often with wreaths, stars and crescent; in 328 the city was renamed Constantina (perhaps in honour of Constantine II, whose seat it was) and the mark becomes CONST (Constantina), later KONSTAN and, under Constans and Constantius, PCON, SCON, TCON. The key identification trap: these CON marks with a Latin officina letter in front belong to Arles, whereas Constantinople writes CONS followed by a Greek officina letter. From the 360s Arles returns to marks such as SCON, TCON, then SMARL. Arles was a major gold mint for the western court in the 5th c. (prefecture of the Gauls moved there c. 407): Constantine III, Jovinus, Valentinian III, Avitus (proclaimed at Arles 455), Majorian and Libius Severus struck solidi and tremisses with AR or A-R flanking the figure, before the Visigothic takeover in 476.

mints.name: Mediolanum (Milan)
mints.notes: Gallienus founded the mint c. 259/260 to pay the new cavalry army based at Milan; antoniniani carry P, S, T or MP, MS, MT and the 'legionary' series honouring individual legions with their badges (LEG II ADIVTRIX VI P VI F) belongs here (a rich collecting series). In 268 Aureolus, besieged at Milan, struck coins in Postumus' name with CONCORD EQVIT and other cavalry-themed reverses. Aurelian moved the mint to Ticinum in 274. Milan reopened for precious metals in the later 4th c. as an imperial residence: MDOB solidi, MDPS siliquae of Valentinian I, Gratian, Valentinian II, Theodosius, Magnus Maximus and Eugenius. Honorius' move to Ravenna (402) reduced it; solidi with M-D in the field continue for 5th-century western emperors (Valentinian III, Majorian, Anthemius) and for Odoacer in Zeno's name.

mints.name: Ticinum (Pavia)
mints.officinae: 3-6; four (P, S, T, Q) normally under the Tetrarchy.
mints.notes: Aurelian transferred the Milan mint here in 274. It struck heavily for Aurelian, Probus (huge variety of bust types, a favourite of specialists: helmeted, cuirassed, with shield and spear, with eagle-tipped sceptre), Carus and family, Diocletian and Maximian, then the Tetrarchic folles (GENIO POPVLI ROMANI) and the coinages of Maxentius and Constantine. Ticinum produced several famous gold multiples and the 315 silver medallion of Constantine with the chi-rho on his helmet (the 'Ticinum medallion'), a key document for his Christian symbolism. Closed in 326, its staff probably moving to Constantinople. A later Ostrogothic and Lombard mint at Pavia belongs to another period.

mints.name: Aquileia
mints.notes: Opened in Diocletian's reform of 294. Aquileia's Tetrarchic folles and Constantinian nummi are common; it struck notable gold for Constantine and Licinius and, in the later 4th century, AQOB solidi and AQPS siliquae for Valentinian I, Gratian, Valentinian II, Theodosius, Magnus Maximus (who held it 387-388) and Eugenius. Theodosius defeated Maximus near Aquileia (388) and Eugenius at the Frigidus nearby (394), and coin output tracks these campaigns. Activity dwindled in the early 5th century; issues for Joannes (423-425) and the Theodosian house are the last. Identification: AQ marks with dots and palm-branch symbols separate many short emissions in the 330s-350s.

mints.name: Ravenna
mints.notes: The mint followed Honorius' court to Ravenna in 402 and became the main western gold mint, striking solidi with R-V in the field for Honorius, Constantius III, Joannes, Valentinian III (the most common western solidus of the century, with VICTORIA AVGGG and the emperor treading on a human-headed serpent), Galla Placidia and Honoria, and the later western emperors to Romulus Augustulus. Odoacer and the Ostrogoths kept it: Theodoric and his successors struck gold in the emperor's name with their monograms on silver and bronze, and the city bronze of the 520s-530s shows a turreted personification with FELIX RAVENNA. After 540 Ravenna was the seat of Byzantine Italy (the exarch from the 580s): Byzantine Ravenna solidi are thin and broad with a neat, linear portrait style; bronze reads RAV or RAVENNA. Distinguishing Ravenna, Rome and Constantinople gold of the 6th-7th c. is a specialist skill: compare portrait proportions, lettering and officina markings with the standard catalogues (DOC, MIB, Hahn).

mints.name: Ostia
mints.notes: A short-lived mint created by Maxentius, probably with workers moved from Carthage when Africa revolted under Domitius Alexander (308). Ostia's folles are among the most beautiful of the age: AETERNITAS AVG N with the Dioscuri and their horses, the she-wolf with twins, CONSERV VRB SVAE with Roma in a hexastyle temple, Ostia personified, and the coinage for Divus Romulus (Maxentius' dead son) with the domed shrine. After Constantine's victory at the Milvian Bridge (312) he struck at Ostia briefly, then moved the staff to Arles in 313. Marks are unambiguous (MOST = Moneta Ostiensis).

mints.name: Carthago (Carthage)
marks: N XLII / N XXI / N XII (Vandal)
mints.notes: Diocletian opened a mint at Carthage c. 296 for the African provinces, with the distinctive types SALVIS AVGG ET CAESS FEL KART (Carthage holding fruit) and FELIX ADVENT AVGG NN for Maximian's African campaign (297/8). It struck for Maxentius after 306, then for the usurper L. Domitius Alexander (308-310), whose folles are rare and much faked, and closed after Maxentius' recovery of Africa (310-311). The Vandals (from 439) struck silver and bronze, at first in the names of Honorius, later with royal names (Gunthamund, Thrasamund, Hilderic, Gelimer) and value marks: silver of 100, 50 and 25 denarii, and bronze of 42, 21 and 12 nummi (N XLII, N XXI, N XII), the latter partly anticipating Anastasius' reform. Justinian's reconquest (533) restored an imperial mint whose output to the 690s is a large and characterful series: small, thick 'globular' gold under Heraclius, folles and half-folles with CAR or KRTG, and 7th-century solidi and silver often carrying indictional dates. Carthage fell to the Arabs in 698.

mints.name: Caesarea Mauretaniae (Cherchell): royal mint of Mauretania
mints.notes: Juba II, raised in Rome and set on the Mauretanian throne by Augustus in 25 BC, struck denarii on the Roman standard with Latin legends for himself and Greek for his wife Cleopatra Selene (daughter of Antony and Cleopatra), with Egyptian motifs (crocodile, Isis crown, sistrum) and his own scholarly interests (elephant, cornucopia). Their son Ptolemy continued, dating coins by regnal year (R A I to R A XX), until Caligula had him killed in 40 and annexed the kingdom. These are among the most attractive client-king denarii; Cleopatra Selene's pieces are scarce and widely faked.

mints.name: Carnuntum: mint of Regalianus
mints.notes: In 260, after the capture of Valerian, the Pannonian commander Regalianus was proclaimed and briefly ruled before being killed. His antoniniani, and those of his wife Sulpicia Dryantilla, were improvised by overstriking old denarii of the Severan age, whose undertypes can often still be read; the flans are small and thick and the engraving crude. Found mainly around Carnuntum, they are attributed to a local emergency mint. All are rare, and modern forgeries exist; an authentic piece should show traces of the host denarius and a crude, provincial style.

mints.name: Siscia (Sisak)
marks: P S T Q V VI (Gallienus-Claudius)
mints.notes: Gallienus opened Siscia c. 262; it became one of the busiest bronze mints of the empire. 3rd-c. radiates carry officina numerals and, after Aurelian's reform, XXI with letters. Its Constantinian and Valentinianic issues are notorious among specialists for an enormous range of field marks (letters, symbols, wreaths, crescents and combinations), which define dozens of small issues of the GLORIA ROMANORVM and SECVRITAS REIPVBLICAE types of 364-378. Siscia struck gold and silver for Licinius and Constantine, Vetranio (350, whose HOC SIGNO VICTOR ERIS bronze with a labarum is struck here and at Thessalonica), Constantius II and the Valentinianic house. Closed c. 387. Identification: Greek officina letters precede SIS (ASIS), whereas Rome and Arles use Latin letters.

mints.name: Sirmium (Sremska Mitrovica)
mints.notes: An imperial residence with an intermittent mint. Constantine opened it c. 320 while preparing for the war with Licinius; it struck CAESARVM NOSTRORVM VOT X and the camp-gate PROVIDENTIAE types and fine gold. Constantius II revived it during the war with Magnentius (351, Mursa was nearby). Valentinian I and Valens struck gold and bronze there in the 360s-370s, and a final burst of solidi and bronzes for Theodosius and his sons came in 393-395. In the 5th-6th centuries Sirmium passed through Hunnic, Gepid and Ostrogothic hands, and some pseudo-imperial Gepid issues are attributed to it. Sirmium coins are scarcer than those of Siscia and Thessalonica.

mints.name: Catania (Byzantine Sicily)
mints.notes: A Byzantine bronze mint in Sicily, opened under Maurice (c. 582) and closed under Heraclius. It struck folles (M), half-folles and smaller pieces with CAT/KAT. Catanian folles of Maurice and Phocas are often of large module but irregular manufacture, and many Heraclian coins in Sicily are overstrikes. Its output was replaced by the Sicilian mint whose coins read SCL (probably at Syracuse).

mints.name: Syracusae: the Byzantine Sicilian mint (SCL)
mints.notes: From late in Heraclius' reign a Sicilian mint marked SCL (Sicilia) struck folles, and later 7th-century gold and silver of a distinctive style is attributed to it. It is normally placed at Syracuse, the island's administrative centre (later briefly the residence of Constans II, 663-668). Sicilian Heraclian folles are often overstruck on older coins, sometimes on coins of other mints, and show Heraclius with his son(s) standing. Most of the mint's history falls after 641.

hoards.name: Mazin Hoard
hoards.contents: Over a thousand pieces of bronze, mostly cut fragments: aes rude, Roman aes signatum bars and aes grave, together with bronze coins of Carthage, Numidia, Ptolemaic Egypt, Syracuse and other Hellenistic states, all treated as bullion by weight.
hoards.significance: Found in the Lika uplands of Croatia, far outside the Roman world of its day, the hoard is the classic demonstration that early Roman bronze and Mediterranean coin travelled as metal by weight in barbarian Europe. It is one of the main sources for the appearance of aes signatum (cast bars with oxen, tridents, branches) and of fragments of aes rude, Rome's pre-coinage money. Its deposit date is not fixed with precision: it is usually placed in the 2nd or early 1st century BC.

hoards.name: Morgantina destruction deposits (Sicily)
hoards.foundNote: excavated from 1955 by Princeton University; key hoards published by Buttrey and others
hoards.contents: Several coin hoards and stray finds sealed by the Roman sack of the city in 211 BC (Livy 26.21), including early denarii, quinarii, victoriati and associated reduced bronze, alongside Syracusan and Punic coins of Hieronymus and the Sicilian republic.
hoards.significance: The most important archaeological evidence for when the denarius began. Before the excavations, the introduction of the denarius was dated variously to 269 (Pliny NH 33.44) or 187 (Mattingly). The Morgantina contexts, ended by the Roman capture of the city during the Second Punic War, contain denarii and so require a date no later than c. 211, which Crawford adopted. The finds are used together with the corn-ear series attributed to a Roman mint in Sicily.

hoards.name: Cosa Hoard
hoards.contents: 2,004 Roman Republican denarii in a pot buried under the floor of a house near the forum of Cosa; the latest coins were dated by T. V. Buttrey to c. 74-72 BC.
hoards.where: Museo Archeologico Nazionale di Cosa (Ansedonia) and American Academy in Rome records
hoards.significance: Buttrey linked the hoard to a destruction of Cosa around 70 BC, which he attributed to the pirate raids that plagued the Tyrrhenian coast before Pompey's command of 67. The hoard's composition is a fixed point for the chronology of the late Republican denarius series, and the debate about its closing date was part of the argument that produced Crawford's revised chronology in RRC (1974). It shows the savings of an ordinary townsman at the time of the Spartacus and Sertorius wars.

hoards.name: Hallaton Treasure
hoards.contents: Over 5,000 coins in some 16 separate deposits (the bulk Iron Age silver and gold of the Corieltavi, plus over 150 Roman denarii, the earliest Republican, the latest of the early Principate), with a silver-gilt Roman cavalry parade helmet, a silver bowl and remains of feasting (pig bones).
hoards.significance: An open-air shrine of the Corieltavi in Leicestershire where coins were buried as offerings around the time of the Claudian invasion. The Roman helmet, possibly a diplomatic gift or the gear of a Briton serving Rome, and the Roman denarii side by side with native coin show the depth of contact before conquest. It is the largest find of Iron Age coins from Britain and changed views of the Corieltavi's wealth.

hoards.name: Bredgar Hoard
hoards.contents: 37 gold aurei from Julius Caesar to Claudius, the latest of AD 41-42.
hoards.significance: Found in Kent close to the line of the invasion army's advance, it has been plausibly interpreted as the savings of a Roman officer who hid it during the campaign of AD 43 and never returned. Small but evocative, it is a rare direct trace of the invasion itself.

hoards.name: Kalkriese battlefield coin finds
hoards.foundNote: first coins found by Major J. A. S. (Tony) Clunn; excavations from 1989
hoards.contents: Several thousand Roman coins scattered over the battlefield: hoards and singles of aurei, many denarii (above all the Gaius and Lucius Caesares type of 2 BC-AD 4) and copper asses, many of them Lugdunum Altar asses and coins countermarked VAR, together with weapons, armour fragments and the famous iron face mask.
hoards.significance: The coins identified the site as the battlefield of the Teutoburg disaster (AD 9). No coin is later than AD 9, the Gaius-Lucius denarius is the latest gold and silver type, and the VAR countermark, applied under Quinctilius Varus' command, ties the bronze to his army. The case is a model of how numismatics locates an event. Debate continues over whether the site represents Varus' defeat or a later Germanicus-era clash (AD 15-16); the coin evidence favours AD 9.

hoards.name: Hildesheim Treasure
hoards.contents: About 70 pieces of Augustan-era silver tableware (the Athena bowl, a large krater, cups and dishes), no coins.
hoards.significance: Found by Prussian soldiers digging a rifle range, the treasure was long romantically connected with Varus or with Germanicus' campaigns. It is most probably Roman plate that reached a Germanic leader as gift, payment or plunder in the Augustan period. Its significance for numismatists is negative: it shows that the richest finds in Free Germany are often plate rather than coin, and that dating must rely on the silverwork.

hoards.name: Boscoreale Treasure
hoards.contents: 109 pieces of silver tableware (including the cups with dancing skeletons and the Augustus and Tiberius triumph cups), gold jewellery and a purse of roughly 1,000 gold aurei with some silver, hidden in the wine-press cistern of the Villa della Pisanella.
hoards.where: Musée du Louvre (silver, given by Baron Edmond de Rothschild); coins dispersed
hoards.significance: Hidden during the eruption of Vesuvius in AD 79, the hoard gives a snapshot of gold in circulation at a dated moment: aurei of Augustus to Vespasian, with Nero's pre- and post-reform coins showing how the lighter post-64 aureus coexisted with older, heavier coins. The aurei were sold on the market, which deprived scholarship of a complete record; the silver is one of the finest Roman services known.

hoards.name: House of the Menander treasure, Pompeii
hoards.contents: 118 pieces of silver plate packed in a chest in the basement of the bath suite, with jewellery and a small sum of gold and silver coins.
hoards.significance: Stored away, probably during repairs to the house, rather than hidden in flight, the silver shows the plate of a rich Pompeian family (perhaps the Poppaei) at the moment of the eruption. The coins with it are a small but securely dated sample of what was in a household's purse in 79, and help calibrate the wear on 1st-century coins.

hoards.name: Snettisham Roman Jeweller's Hoard
hoards.contents: A pot holding 110 engraved carnelian intaglios, silver and gold rings and bracelets, scrap silver, jeweller's tools and 83 silver denarii, the latest of the mid-2nd century (c. 155).
hoards.significance: The working stock of a provincial jeweller in Norfolk: the coins were silver bullion for his craft as much as money. It documents how denarii were melted down for jewellery, the local production of finger rings in the Antonine period, and the imagery chosen by Romano-British customers on gemstones.

hoards.name: Didcot Hoard
hoards.contents: 126 gold aurei from Nero to Antoninus Pius, in a pot.
hoards.significance: Worth perhaps a decade of a legionary's pay, it is one of the larger gold hoards from Roman Britain. Its range shows how long aurei circulated (Neronian coins over 90 years old), and the absence of debasement in gold contrasts with the gradual decline of the denarius in the same decades.

hoards.name: Trier Gold Hoard
hoards.contents: 2,650 gold aurei, c. 18.5 kg, from Nero to Septimius Severus, the latest c. 196.
hoards.significance: The largest Roman gold hoard ever found, uncovered by a mechanical digger in Feldstraße; some coins were taken by onlookers and later recovered. Hidden around the time of the civil war between Septimius Severus and Clodius Albinus (196-197), when Trier lay in Albinus' sphere, it may be a public or temple treasury rather than private wealth. It is a fundamental sample for the 2nd-century aureus: types, die combinations, and wear.

hoards.name: Shapwick Hoard
hoards.contents: 9,262 silver denarii from Mark Antony's legionary issues to Severus Alexander (c. 224), probably originally in a bag or box in the floor of a room.
hoards.significance: The largest hoard of denarii from Britain. Its discovery led to the identification of a previously unknown Roman villa. It shows the denarius still being saved after Caracalla's antoninianus had appeared (215), with Antony's debased legionary denarii still in circulation 250 years after Actium, and gives a large sample for the late Severan denarius.

hoards.name: Dura-Europos siege hoards
hoards.contents: More than a dozen hoards of antoniniani, Antiochene billon tetradrachms and bronze, the latest of the mid-250s, found in houses, towers and the wall embankment.
hoards.significance: The hoards were abandoned when the Sasanian army of Shapur I took the city (c. 256), and they fix the date of the siege. They show the coins in the pockets of the garrison and townspeople, the mix of imperial and provincial money in the East, and the speed of debasement in the 250s. Bellinger's publication (Excavations at Dura-Europos, Final Report VI) remains a standard source.

hoards.name: Réka Devnia Hoard
hoards.contents: About 81,000 silver denarii and antoniniani (figures between c. 80,000 and 100,000 are cited), from Mark Antony to Trajan Decius, the latest of 250-251.
hoards.where: Regional Historical Museum, Varna (bulk); part dispersed on the market
hoards.significance: The largest silver hoard of the Roman Empire, found near ancient Marcianopolis in Moesia Inferior and published by N. Mouchmov (1934). It was hidden during the Gothic invasion of Cniva (250-251) that ended with the death of Decius at Abritus. Because of its size it became the statistical basis for estimating the relative rarity of 2nd- and 3rd-century denarii, and its distribution of types informs RIC's rarity ratings and studies of mint output (for example the ratio of issues for emperors and empresses).

hoards.name: Eauze Treasure
hoards.contents: About 28,000 coins (mostly antoniniani and denarii), together with some 50 pieces of gold jewellery, precious stones and a few silver objects.
hoards.significance: Found in the ancient city of Elusa in Aquitania during construction work, it was hidden around the time of the Gallic secession of Postumus (260), when barbarian raids and civil war struck Gaul. It is one of the largest treasure finds from France and shows the scale of private wealth held in coin in a provincial town on the eve of the crisis.

hoards.name: Lyon-Vaise Treasure
hoards.contents: Silver statuettes of deities, gold and silver jewellery and tableware, with coins closing around the mid-3rd century.
hoards.significance: A rich household treasure from a suburb of Lyon hidden in the turmoil around 260. The silver statuettes, perhaps from a domestic shrine, are rare survivals. With Eauze, Chaourse and others, it belongs to a well-defined horizon of Gallic hoards around 260 that marks the collapse of security in the decade of Valerian's capture.

hoards.name: Chaourse Treasure
hoards.contents: 39 pieces of silver tableware (dishes, a statuette of Mercury, cups) found with coins reaching the 260s.
hoards.significance: A Gaulish household service of the 2nd-3rd centuries buried near Montcornet (Aisne) around the time of the Gallic Empire. The coins date the deposit and place it in the same horizon of insecurity as the Mâcon, Eauze and Lyon-Vaise treasures.

hoards.name: Beau Street Hoard (Bath)
hoards.contents: 17,577 silver and base-silver coins (denarii from 32 BC and radiates to c. 274) packed in at least eight separate bags, deposited together in a stone-lined pit.
hoards.significance: Excavated as a single block and micro-excavated in the British Museum, the hoard preserved the bag groupings, which proved to be sorted by denomination and date. This revealed how a Roman owner managed savings in a period of debasement, keeping older good-silver denarii apart from the near-worthless radiates of the Gallic emperors.

hoards.name: Cunetio Hoard
hoards.contents: 54,951 radiates and some denarii in a lead-lined box and pot, from the 250s to Aurelian's early reformed coinage (274-275).
hoards.significance: Found at Mildenhall (Wiltshire), the site of the Roman small town of Cunetio, it was the largest coin hoard ever found in Britain until Frome. Its exhaustive publication by E. Besly and R. Bland (The Cunetio Treasure, 1983) established the internal chronology of the Gallic Empire coinages of Postumus, Victorinus and the Tetrici, and documented the transition at the moment of Aurelian's reunification and coin reform.

hoards.name: Neupotz Hoard
hoards.contents: Over 1,000 objects, roughly 700 kg of metal: bronze cauldrons and vessels, iron tools, agricultural implements, silver tableware, votive objects and some coins of the 270s.
hoards.significance: The loot of an Alamannic war band returning from raids deep in Gaul, lost while crossing the Rhine, probably in the 270s. It shows what raiders valued (metal of every kind, not only silver) and how the barbarian invasions of the 3rd century looked from the side of the raiders. Related finds come from Hagenbach. Its coins date the event and connect it with the invasions that followed the fall of the Gallic Empire (275-277), which Probus had to repel.

hoards.name: Normanby Hoard
hoards.contents: 47,912 radiates in a pot, the latest of Carausius (c. 289).
hoards.significance: Published by R. Bland and A. Burnett (1988), it is a principal source for the chronology of Carausius' early coinage and for what was circulating in Britain after the break with the central empire. Like Cunetio, it consists overwhelmingly of irregular and official base radiates of the Gallic and central emperors.

hoards.name: Frome Hoard
hoards.contents: 52,503 coins in a single large pot, from c. 253 to Carausius (c. 290), including 766 coins of Carausius and five of his rare silver denarii.
hoards.significance: Found by metal detectorist Dave Crisp and excavated by archaeologists, the hoard showed that the coins had been poured into a pot already buried in the ground, in batches, and that the pot could not be emptied without breaking it: strong evidence that it was a ritual deposit rather than recoverable savings. It is the largest single-pot hoard from Britain and changed the debate about the motives behind 3rd-century hoarding.

hoards.name: Venèra Hoard
hoards.contents: Over 46,000 base-silver radiates of the mid- to late 3rd century, the latest of the Tetrarchic period just before Diocletian's reform.
hoards.where: Museo di Castelvecchio and Verona museums (part); dispersed
hoards.significance: Found at Venèra near Sanguinetto (Verona), it is the largest Italian hoard of the period. It is one of the main reference finds for the coinage of the Gallic and central emperors of 260-294 and for the circulation of reformed aureliani in northern Italy.

hoards.name: Beaurains (Arras) Treasure
hoards.contents: Gold coins (several hundred aurei and solidi), about 25 gold medallions, silver vessels, ingots and jewellery; the latest coins of c. 310-315. Most famous piece: the gold medallion of Constantius I showing his arrival at London (LON) in 296, legend REDDITOR LVCIS AETERNAE.
hoards.where: Musée des Beaux-Arts, Arras; British Museum; other museums (the treasure was largely dispersed)
hoards.significance: Found by workmen near Arras, it was illegally dispersed and only partly recovered. It is the accumulated imperial gifts of a high officer, given at accessions and anniversaries over two decades (medallions for vota, consulships and victories). The Arras medallion of Constantius I, struck at Trier, is the earliest depiction of London (a kneeling figure before the city gate, a galley on the Thames) and the most important single document for the recovery of Britain from Allectus in 296.

hoards.name: Tomares Hoard
hoards.contents: 19 amphorae containing an estimated 600 kg of bronze nummi of the late 3rd and early 4th century (Maximian to Constantine).
hoards.significance: Found by workmen laying pipes in a park near Seville. Many coins appear unworn, which suggests a consignment of fresh money (tax revenue, army pay or a payment to a contractor) rather than private savings. It illustrates the scale of state bronze issues under the Tetrarchy and Constantine, when the nummus was repeatedly reduced and huge volumes moved in containers.

hoards.name: Misurata Hoard
hoards.contents: About 108,000 bronze coins (nummi) of the Tetrarchic and Constantinian period, stored in jars.
hoards.where: Libya (Department of Antiquities); restored in Italy by the CNR Institute for Technologies Applied to Cultural Heritage
hoards.significance: Found by chance near Misurata (ancient Thubactis region of Tripolitania), it is often called the largest coin hoard ever found by number of coins. Its restoration (completed c. 2009) required new cleaning methods. It shows the massive volumes of small bronze needed in early 4th-century North Africa and the cash flows of a coastal Tripolitanian economy then dominated by olive oil.

hoards.name: Seaton Down Hoard
hoards.contents: 22,888 copper-alloy nummi, the latest of c. 348.
hoards.significance: Found by metal detectorist Laurence Egerton near the Honeyditches villa in Devon, it is one of the largest 4th-century hoards from Britain. It closes just before the FEL TEMP REPARATIO reform of 348, when the old small coins were superseded, which may explain why it was never recovered: its contents lost value overnight.

hoards.name: Kaiseraugst Treasure
hoards.contents: A silver service of over 60 vessels and utensils (the Achilles plate, the Ariadne dish, a candelabrum), 186 coins and medallions, and 3 silver ingots stamped with the name and portrait of Magnentius; a further group of 18 pieces surfaced from the finder's estate in 1995.
hoards.significance: Buried at the fortress of Castrum Rauracense on the Rhine during the civil war of Magnentius and Alamannic invasions (c. 351-352). The coins and the ingots (largesse given to officers) suggest that the owner was a high-ranking officer in Magnentius' service. It is a key example of imperial largesse in precious metal and of the luxury plate of the 4th-century military elite.

hoards.name: Water Newton Treasure and gold hoard
hoards.contents: 27 silver objects (bowls, a cup, a strainer and votive plaques), many with the chi-rho, found in 1975; in 1974 a separate hoard of 30 gold solidi of the mid-4th century was found in the same field at Durobrivae.
hoards.significance: The earliest known group of Christian liturgical silver from the Roman Empire. The votive leaf plaques, a pagan custom adapted to Christian use, and inscriptions such as 'Publianus' and 'Innocentia et Viventia' show a Christian congregation in a small town of Britain. The nearby solidus hoard is a reminder of the wealth in gold that the new Constantinian coinage put into the hands of local elites.

hoards.name: Mildenhall Treasure
hoards.contents: 34 pieces of 4th-century silver tableware, including the Great Dish (Oceanus dish, c. 8.3 kg) with Bacchic revels, platters, bowls with lids, goblets and spoons, three with the chi-rho. No coins.
hoards.significance: Found by a ploughman at West Row near Mildenhall (Suffolk) and kept secret until 1946. It has no coins, so it is dated by style to the mid-4th century; Greek inscriptions on two platters (Eutherios) have suggested a link with Eutherius, chamberlain of Julian. Its pagan imagery side by side with Christian spoons shows the mixed culture of the 4th-century elite. Some scholars have doubted that it was buried in Britain in antiquity, but the find circumstances are now generally accepted.

hoards.name: Szilágysomlyó (Şimleu Silvaniei) Treasure
hoards.contents: Gold medallions of 4th-century emperors from Maximian to Gratian (including very large multiples of Valens and Valentinian I), many set in frames as pendants, with gold chains, brooches, rings and vessels.
hoards.where: Kunsthistorisches Museum, Vienna (1797 find); Hungarian National Museum, Budapest (1889 find)
hoards.significance: Imperial gold medallions were diplomatic and military gifts. Here they reached a Germanic (probably Gepid) ruling family beyond the Danube and were turned into insignia of status. The treasure documents the flow of Roman gold to barbarian elites in the late 4th and 5th centuries and the prestige of the imperial image outside the empire.

hoards.name: Thetford Treasure
hoards.contents: 81 items: 22 gold finger rings, bracelets, necklaces, a gold belt buckle with a dancing satyr, unused gems, and 33 silver spoons and strainers, many inscribed to the god Faunus with Celtic epithets (Medigenus, Narius, Auseci and others). No coins.
hoards.significance: Found by a metal detectorist at Gallows Hill, Thetford. The jewellery is unworn stock, perhaps a jeweller's or a cult's treasury. The spoons reveal an otherwise unknown late Roman cult of Faunus in Britain, active in the later 4th century when pagan worship was being restricted by imperial law. The controversy over the find and its reporting contributed to the reform of English treasure law (Treasure Act 1996).

hoards.name: Hoxne Hoard
hoards.contents: 14,865 coins (569 gold solidi, 14,272 silver coins, mostly siliquae with some miliarenses, and 24 bronze nummi), the latest of Constantine III (407-408), with about 200 items of gold and silver: jewellery including a body chain and a bracelet inscribed VTERE FELIX DOMINA IVLIANE, and tableware including the 'Empress' pepper pot and a tigress handle.
hoards.significance: Found by Eric Lawes looking for a lost hammer, and excavated professionally the next day, so that its packing in a wooden chest was recorded. It is the largest late Roman hoard of gold and silver from anywhere in the empire. Nearly all the siliquae are clipped, the best evidence for the clipping of silver in early 5th-century Britain, probably to extract bullion as new coin stopped arriving. Names on the objects (Aurelius Ursicinus, Juliane) point to a wealthy family burying its portable wealth at the end of Roman rule in Britain, when the latest coins are those of the usurper Constantine III.

hoards.name: Traprain Law Treasure
hoards.contents: About 23 kg of late Roman silver plate, mostly cut and folded into hacksilver (bowls, flagons, spoons, some with Christian symbols), with four silver siliquae, the latest of Honorius.
hoards.significance: Found on the hillfort of the Votadini in East Lothian, beyond Hadrian's Wall. The deliberate cutting of fine Roman plate into pieces of weight shows silver used as bullion currency, probably payments or subsidies to friendly northern leaders (or plunder). It belongs to a group of hacksilver finds from Scotland, Ireland and Free Germany around 400-450 that show Roman silver turning into a barbarian currency as coin supply ended.

hoards.name: Ballinrees (Coleraine) Hoard
hoards.contents: 1,506 silver coins (siliquae, many clipped, with a few miliarenses), about 200 oz of silver ingots and hacksilver from cut-up plate; the latest coins of the early 5th century.
hoards.significance: The largest Roman find from Ireland. Whether it represents Irish raiding on Britain, payment for mercenaries or trade, it shows Roman silver crossing the Irish Sea at the very end of Roman Britain. Its clipped siliquae match the British pattern seen at Hoxne.

hoards.name: Szikáncs Hoard
hoards.contents: 1,439 gold solidi, almost all of Theodosius II, the latest of c. 443.
hoards.significance: Found near Hódmezővásárhely on the Hungarian plain, the heartland of Attila's Huns, it is a physical trace of the huge sums the eastern court paid to the Huns: Priscus records 6,000 lb of gold in arrears and 2,100 lb a year from 447. The predominance of Constantinopolitan solidi struck around 443 suggests a single tribute payment.

hoards.name: Patching Hoard
hoards.contents: 23 gold solidi and about 30 silver siliquae with two miliarenses, scrap silver and rings; the latest coins are solidi of Libius Severus (461-465), and the hoard includes Visigothic imitations.
hoards.significance: The latest Roman coin hoard found in Britain, deposited around 470. It proves that late western gold and silver still reached south-east Britain two generations after the end of Roman rule, perhaps through contacts with Gaul. Its clipped siliquae continue the British practice seen at Hoxne.

hoards.name: Öland, Gotland and Bornholm solidus hoards
hoards.foundNote: many finds from the 18th century to the present
hoards.contents: Several hundred late 5th-century solidi in dozens of hoards, mostly of Leo I, Zeno and Anastasius, from both eastern and western mints, many pierced or looped.
hoards.where: Swedish History Museum, Stockholm; National Museum of Denmark
hoards.significance: The Baltic islands hold the largest concentration of 5th-century solidi outside the empire. They are usually explained as pay or plunder brought home by Scandinavian warriors serving in the armies and war bands of the post-Attila period (Odoacer's Italy, the Ostrogoths, the eastern field armies). Die studies link many to specific western mints such as Ravenna and Milan. They offer a rare view of the empire's gold from the far periphery.

hoards.name: South Indian denarius hoards (Coimbatore, Pudukkottai and others)
hoards.foundNote: dozens of finds since the 18th century
hoards.contents: Thousands of Roman denarii and some aurei, overwhelmingly of Augustus and Tiberius (the Gaius-Lucius and PONTIF MAXIM types), many with deliberate slash or chisel cuts across the portrait.
hoards.where: Government Museum, Chennai; British Museum; other collections
hoards.significance: Physical evidence of the Indian Ocean trade described in the Periplus Maris Erythraei and the Muziris papyrus: Roman silver and gold went to the Tamil kingdoms for pepper, pearls and textiles, as Pliny complained (NH 6.101, 12.84). The preference for early 1st-century coins of good silver, and their cutting (whether testing or demonetising), show the coins valued as bullion, not as Roman money. Neronian debasement after 64 coincides with a falling-off of denarii in India.

hoards.name: Sion Treasure (Kumluca)
hoards.contents: About 50 pieces of church silver (patens, chalices, censers, lamps, book covers) from the monastery of Holy Sion in Lycia, many with imperial control stamps of the reign of Justinian.
hoards.where: Antalya Archaeological Museum; Dumbarton Oaks, Washington
hoards.significance: Not a coin hoard, but its silver carries the official control stamps (five stamps naming the emperor and officials) used under Justinian to guarantee the purity of silver, part of the same state metal control as the coinage. It shows how wealth was stored in church plate in the 6th century, a reserve that Heraclius later melted for coin to pay for the Persian war (622).

hoards.name: Sutton Hoo Mound 1 coins
hoards.contents: 37 Merovingian gold tremisses, each from a different mint, with three blank flans and two small ingots, in the purse from the ship burial.
hoards.significance: The coins, minted in Frankish Gaul in imitation of the late Roman tremissis, date the burial to the 620s and so support identification with King Rædwald of East Anglia (died c. 624). The careful choice of 37 different mints plus blanks has been read as payment for 40 ghostly oarsmen. They show how the Roman gold coinage system survived in the successor kingdoms.

hoards.name: Malaya Pereshchepina Treasure
hoards.contents: About 25 kg of gold and 50 kg of silver objects, including Byzantine and Sasanian silver plate, weapons, jewellery and around 70 Byzantine solidi from Maurice to the 640s (with imitations).
hoards.significance: Found near Poltava in Ukraine and generally identified as the grave or treasure of Kubrat, ruler of the Onogur Bulgars and an ally of Heraclius (who gave him the title of patrician, according to the Short History of Nikephoros). The Byzantine coins and plate are the diplomatic gifts by which Constantinople bought allies on the steppe while fighting Persia and the Avars. A monogram ring has been read as Kubrat's name.

hoards.name: Lambousa treasures (First and Second Cyprus Treasures)
hoards.contents: Byzantine silver plate including the nine David Plates (stamped with control marks of 613-629/30), gold jewellery and a girdle with gold coins and medallions; coins of the 6th-7th centuries.
hoards.where: Metropolitan Museum of Art, New York; Cyprus Museum, Nicosia; British Museum
hoards.significance: Hidden at Lapithos in northern Cyprus during the Arab raids of the 650s. The David Plates, made in Constantinople under Heraclius, have been read as an allegory of his victory over Khosrow II (David and Goliath), and their control stamps date them. The jewellery with mounted coins and medallions shows coin as ornament and wealth store in the last generation of Roman Cyprus.

coinage.standard: aureus 1/40 lb (c. 7.9-8.0 g) = 25 denarii; denarius 1/84 lb (c. 3.9 g), c. 97-98% silver; sestertius (orichalcum, c. 25-27 g) = 4 asses; dupondius (orichalcum) = 2 asses; as (copper) = 1/16 denarius
coinage.text: Augustus turned the improvised coinages of the civil wars into a system that lasted 250 years. Gold became a regular denomination, fixed at 25 denarii. From c. 23 BC the moneyers at Rome again struck base metal, now in two alloys whose colour marked value: yellow orichalcum (brass, a zinc-copper alloy produced by cementation) for the sestertius and dupondius, red copper for the as and quadrans. The quadrans was the price of a bath. The moneyers' names (IIIVIR AAAFF) appear around a large SC until c. 4 BC, after which aes carries the emperor's portrait. Gold and silver moved to Lugdunum c. 15 BC. In the provinces, Augustus allowed cities and colonies to keep their own bronze and the East its silver (cistophori, Alexandrian tetradrachms, Antiochene tetradrachms), producing the dual system of 'imperial' and 'provincial' coinage that collectors still use. Values for prices: a legionary was paid 225 denarii a year (900 sesterces) until Domitian.
scholarship: Burnett, Amandry and Ripollès, Roman Provincial Coinage I (1992)

coinage.t: What does SC on imperial bronze mean?
coinage.text: From the Augustan reform to the 260s almost all Rome-mint bronze bears SC (senatus consulto), while gold and silver do not. The old view (Mommsen) was that the Senate controlled bronze and the emperor precious metals. Most numismatists now reject a division of minting authority: the formula refers to a senatorial decree authorising the issue, honouring the emperor, or legitimising the token value of the base-metal coinage, and the emperor controlled the whole mint. SC also appears on Antioch's bronze, struck for the governor of Syria. Its disappearance in the 260s, with the end of the sestertius, marks the death of the Augustan system.
scholarship: Burnett, 'The authority to coin in the late Republic and early Empire', NC 1977

coinage.text: TI CAESAR DIVI AVG F AVGVSTVS / PONTIF MAXIM, a seated woman holding sceptre and branch (often identified as Livia as Pax or Iustitia). Struck at Lugdunum in great numbers through Tiberius' reign, it is traditionally identified with the denarius shown to Jesus in the Gospels ('Whose image and inscription is this?', Mark 12.13-17). Whether this particular type or older denarii of Augustus circulated in Judaea in the 30s is uncertain, but the identification has made it one of the most collected ancient coins. Three main variants exist by the chair's legs (plain or ornate) and the presence of a footstool; ornate-leg types are earlier. Many modern fakes and ancient plated copies.
scholarship: Giard, Le monnayage de l'atelier de Lyon (1983)

coinage.text: Small stamps punched into circulating bronze revalidated, recalled or advertised. VAR on asses in Germany belongs to Quinctilius Varus (6-9) and helped identify Kalkriese; IMP AVG and AVG on Altar asses and Nemausus coins; TIB, TIB AVG and TIB IMP on Augustan coins in the Rhine camps; NCAPR (debated: Nero Claudius Augustus Probavit?) on Claudian and Neronian aes in Italy; PROB and BON(um) as approval marks; SPQR, IMP VES and other marks in the civil war of 68-69 (Galba and Vespasian's partisans validating old coins and erasing the names of Caligula, whose coins were defaced after his assassination). Countermarks are a primary source for circulation, military pay and political memory, and specialist studies (Werz, Pangerl) exploit them.
scholarship: Werz, Gegenstempel auf Aes-Prägungen der frühen römischen Kaiserzeit (2009)

coinage.standard: aureus cut from 1/40 to 1/45 lb (c. 7.3 g); denarius from 1/84 to 1/96 lb (c. 3.4 g) and fineness reduced (Walker c. 93%; Butcher and Ponting c. 80%)
coinage.text: In the year of the Great Fire, Nero reduced the weight of gold and silver and, on recent metallurgical analysis (Butcher and Ponting 2014), cut the fineness of the denarius much more than Walker's surface analyses implied, probably also adding silver from older coins recalled and restruck. Pliny notes the lighter aureus. At the same time the mint, back at Rome after decades at Lugdunum, began a remarkable bronze programme: experimental orichalcum asses and semisses, value marks (II on dupondii, I on asses), and some of the finest portrait sestertii ever struck, with types of the harbour of Ostia (PORT AVG), the Temple of Janus closed (PACE P R TERRA MARIQ PARTA IANVM CLVSIT), the Macellum Magnum and the Congiarium. Why it matters: it is the first deliberate debasement of the imperial silver, a fiscal response to the costs of rebuilding Rome and the Golden House, and it set the denarius on its long path of decline.
scholarship: Butcher and Ponting, The Metallurgy of Roman Silver Coinage (2014)
MacDowall, The Western Coinages of Nero (1979)

coinage.text: Between Vindex's revolt (spring 68) and Vespasian's victory (December 69) Gaul, Spain, Africa and the Rhine produced coins with no emperor's portrait, the so-called 'autonomous' issues: SIGNA P R, GENIO P R, FIDES EXERCITVVM, SALVS GENERIS HVMANI, LIBERTAS RESTITVTA, ROMA RENASC. Some belong to Vindex and his allies in Gaul, some to Galba in Spain, some to the German legions before they proclaimed Vitellius, and one rare group to L. Clodius Macer, legate of Africa, with his bare head and PRO PRAE AFRICAE. They give a unique view of Republican and military slogans in a war between armies. All are rare to very rare, and attribution of individual groups is debated (Martin, Kraay).
scholarship: Martin, Die anonymen Münzen des Jahres 68 nach Christus (1974)
Kraay, 'The coinage of Vindex and Galba', NC 1949

coinage.text: Vespasian and Titus celebrated the suppression of the Jewish revolt and the destruction of the Temple (70) with one of the longest-running victory series in Roman coinage. Typical sestertius: a Jewess seated mourning beneath a palm, with the emperor or a bound Jewish captive standing, IVDAEA CAPTA S C. Denarii read IVDAEA under a mourning figure, with a trophy. Greek-legend versions (IOYΔAIAΣ EAΛΩKYIAΣ) were struck at Caesarea Maritima. The series is iconographically linked with the reliefs of the Arch of Titus. Very popular; sestertii in good condition are expensive and frequently faked or tooled.
scholarship: Meshorer, A Treasury of Jewish Coins (2001)

coinage.t: Domitian restores the silver (82) and partially retreats (85)
coinage.standard: 82-85: denarius c. 3.5 g at about 98% silver (Augustan purity); 85 on: c. 3.4 g at about 92%
coinage.text: Early in his reign Domitian raised the fineness of the denarius back to Augustan standards and the weight of the aureus, an extraordinary act among emperors. In 85 or soon after, when he raised legionary pay by a third (from 300 to 400 denarii, or 900 to 1,200 sesterces), he lowered the silver to roughly the post-64 level. His denarii are therefore a test case for the relationship between army pay, bullion supply and coin quality. Domitianic denarii from 82-85 can sometimes be recognised by their brighter silver and are dated by his consulships (COS VIII-XI) and tribunician years. His long Minerva series (four reverse types repeated annually) makes his denarii easy to date by legend.
scholarship: Carradice, Coinage and Finances in the Reign of Domitian (1983)

coinage.t: Restored coins: Titus, Domitian, Nerva and Trajan
coinage.text: The Flavians and Nerva re-struck earlier imperial bronze types with an added legend REST (restituit), honouring Augustus, Agrippa, Livia, Drusus, Germanicus, Claudius and Galba: a programme of dynastic memory. Trajan went further around 107, issuing restored denarii and aurei of Republican moneyers' types (from the Dioscuri to Caesar's) and of earlier emperors, each with IMP CAES TRAIAN AVG GER DAC P P REST. This came with Trajan's recall and melting of worn old coin reported by Dio. Restored issues are rare to very rare and attractive to collectors of both Republic and Empire; beware tooling and modern fantasy 'restitutions'.
scholarship: Komnick, Die Restitutionsmünzen der frühen Kaiserzeit (2001)
Woytek, Die Reichsprägung des Kaisers Traianus (2010)

coinage.standard: fineness reduced from c. 90% to c. 80% (Butcher and Ponting)
coinage.text: Cassius Dio says that Trajan 'melted down all the worn coinage'. Hoard evidence shows the disappearance of pre-64 denarii in the decades after, and analyses show a fall in fineness at the same date, implying that Trajan profited from the recoinage after the Dacian wars, despite the vast Dacian booty claimed by later sources (John Lydus, citing Crito, of 5 million pounds of gold, a figure no one believes). The 'restored' issues of c. 107 commemorated the coins being withdrawn. Trajan's own denarius types celebrate Dacia, the Forum and Column, the Via Traiana and the Danube bridge.
scholarship: Woytek, Die Reichsprägung des Kaisers Traianus (2010)

coinage.text: During his eastern tour Hadrian ordered a massive recoinage of the silver of Asia Minor at several mints, producing cistophori with cult images of individual cities: Artemis of Ephesus, the temple of Zeus at Pergamum, the Capitoline temple, Diana Lucifera, the image of the city of Nicomedia. Many were overstruck on older cistophori of Antony, Augustus and Claudius, whose undertypes are often visible. It is a key source for Hadrian's dealings with the Greek cities and for provincial cults. Metcalf's die study is the standard work.

coinage.standard: denarius fineness falling from c. 80% (early Pius) to c. 75% (Marcus) and c. 70% (Commodus) on traditional figures
coinage.text: The fineness of the denarius slipped through the 2nd century and fell more sharply under Marcus Aurelius during the Marcomannic wars and the Antonine plague, when the emperor famously auctioned palace treasures in the Forum of Trajan to pay for the war rather than raise taxes (HA Marcus 17). Commodus cut the weight in 186-187. The silver supply from Spain declined in the same period, and many scholars link the debasement with the plague's impact on mining and taxation. Absolute numbers depend on the analytical method: Walker's figures are higher than modern bulk analyses.
scholarship: Walker, The Metrology of the Roman Silver Coinage III (1978)
Duncan-Jones, Money and Government in the Roman Empire (1994)

coinage.standard: denarius at roughly 50% silver from c. 194-196
coinage.text: To pay for the civil wars against Niger and Albinus and for his army pay rise (from 300 to about 450-500 denarii a year), Severus cut the denarius to around half silver: the largest single debasement since its creation. Dio and Herodian record his maxim to his sons, 'enrich the soldiers'. Severan denarii are plentiful, with a wide range of portraits of the family (Julia Domna, Caracalla and Geta as boys) and eastern mint styles. The low-grade silver means that Severan denarii often show copper patches or a grey surface. The debasement made old good-silver denarii worth hoarding: the Shapwick and Réka Devnia hoards show how Gresham's law operated.

coinage.standard: antoninianus c. 5.1 g (one and a half denarii in weight) at about 50% silver, probably tariffed at two denarii; aureus cut to 1/50 lb (c. 6.5 g)
coinage.text: In 215 Caracalla introduced a new silver coin, distinguished by the emperor's radiate crown (and, for empresses, a crescent under the bust), the double-value marks also used on the dupondius. Its ancient name is unknown: 'antoninianus' is a modern coinage from a phrase in the Historia Augusta. Since it weighed only 1.5 denarii but was worth 2, it was a disguised debasement to fund his pay rise and wars. Elagabalus abandoned it c. 219; Pupienus and Balbinus revived it in 238 and under Gordian III it replaced the denarius as the main silver coin, the denarius ceasing as a regular coin by c. 241. The radiate crown is thus the key to recognising the double denomination in the 3rd century, including radiate dupondii and double sestertii.
scholarship: Abdy and others, RIC IV / revisions
Bland, 'Coinage and currency in the 3rd century', in The Roman Imperial Coinage: an Introduction (2012)

coinage.t: The unstable gold of the 3rd century
coinage.text: After Caracalla's aureus at 1/50 lb, gold weights became erratic. Gordian III and Philip struck aurei around 4.5-5 g; under Trebonianus, Valerian and Gallienus weights ran from under 1 g to over 7 g, suggesting gold was valued by weight rather than face. Gallienus also struck radiate binios (double aurei) and spectacular gold multiples. Postumus' gold from the Gallic mints was the best of the period. Aurelian restored an aureus near 1/50 lb; Diocletian set it at 1/60 lb (marked Ξ on some coins), and Constantine's solidus at 1/72 lb ended the instability. Third-century gold is rare and expensive; die studies show that much of it was struck for donatives and largesse to the army.
scholarship: Bland, 'The development of gold and silver coin denominations, AD 193-253', in King and Wigg (eds.) 1996
Callu, La politique monétaire des empereurs romains de 238 à 311 (1969)

coinage.t: The double sestertius and the end of the sestertius
coinage.text: Trajan Decius introduced a radiate double sestertius (c. 250), heavier than the sestertius and marked by the radiate crown, perhaps to restore the value of the bronze as the silver collapsed. Postumus revived it in Gaul (260s) with a superb series of large radiate pieces, often struck on old sestertii. Ordinary sestertii shrank and grew rarer through the 250s and ended under Gallienus; Aurelian struck a last small issue. The disappearance of SC bronze in the 260s, along with the city coinages of the East, marks the end of the Augustan currency system and the reduction of the whole system to a single debased radiate coin.
scholarship: Bastien, Le monnayage de bronze de Postume (1967)
Estiot, 'Aurélien et Tacite', in Ripostiglio della Venèra (1995)

coinage.t: The great debasement of the antoninianus
coinage.standard: c. 45-50% silver under Gordian III; c. 40% under Philip; falling to about 15% under Valerian and to 2-5% under Gallienus' sole reign (260-268); 1-2% under Claudius II and Quintillus
coinage.text: As military crises multiplied, the radiate coin was debased step by step. Under Valerian and Gallienus the decline turned into a collapse; by the late 260s antoniniani were bronze coins with a thin silver wash applied by surface enrichment (blanching), which wears off quickly and gives the dark look of most coins of the period. Coins were also struck on smaller, more irregular flans and in vastly greater numbers at more mints (Milan, Siscia, Cyzicus, the Gallic mints). Prices in Egyptian papyri jump after c. 270, suggesting that confidence finally broke. For collectors this period offers huge variety at low cost, with the challenge of finding coins with their silvering intact. Hoards such as Cunetio, Normanby and Frome are the main evidence.
scholarship: Rathbone, 'Monetisation, not price-inflation, in third-century AD Egypt?', in King and Wigg (eds.) 1996

coinage.t: The end of the civic and provincial coinages
coinage.text: Hundreds of Greek cities had struck their own bronze under Rome. Production peaked under the Severans and in the 240s, then fell away in the 250s and 260s: the last widespread civic issues date to Gallienus, and the very last, at Perge and Side in Pamphylia, to Tacitus (275-276). Alexandria kept its tetradrachms until Diocletian's reform (296/7). The causes debated include the debasement of the imperial radiate (which made civic bronze uneconomic), the cost of festivals, and changes in the cities' finances. The disappearance of the civic coinages removed a vast store of local imagery (temples, festivals, river gods) and a key source on civic titles.
scholarship: Howgego, Heuchert and Burnett (eds.), Coinage and Identity in the Roman Provinces (2005)

coinage.t: Alexandrian tetradrachms and the closed currency of Egypt
coinage.standard: billon tetradrachm c. 12-13 g, falling to c. 8 g; silver c. 25% under Tiberius to under 1% in the 270s
coinage.text: Egypt kept a currency of its own, exchanged at the border. Tetradrachms resumed under Tiberius in AD 19/20 and were dated by regnal year (L + numeral), which makes them precisely dated documents. Big bronze drachms of Antoninus Pius with zodiac signs, Hercules' labours and Nilotic scenes are a celebrated series. Under Claudius II and Aurelian the tetradrachm became nearly pure bronze. Diocletian's reform ended the system c. 296/7, a change that, with the revolt of Domitius Domitianus and Achilleus in 297-298, may reflect resistance to new taxes. Tetradrachms are common (they turn up in huge hoards) and an excellent, cheap way to collect 3rd-century portraits including obscure emperors.
scholarship: Christiansen, The Roman Coins of Alexandria (1988)
Geissen and Weiser, Katalog alexandrinischer Kaisermünzen (Cologne, 1974-1983)

coinage.text: In Britain and northern Gaul the coins of Tetricus I and II and Claudius II's DIVO CLAVDIO consecration issues were copied on a massive scale in the 270s-280s, producing 'barbarous radiates' from near-official size down to tiny 'minims' a few millimetres across. They fill the gap left by the demonetisation of Gallic coin after Aurelian's reform and before Carausius' coinage. Their crude, often fantastic designs (garbled legends, stick-figure reverses) make them a cult collecting area. Similar waves of imitation followed later: copies of the FEL TEMP REPARATIO falling horseman (350s), and 'minimissimi' in 5th-century Britain and the Mediterranean.
scholarship: Boon, 'Counterfeit coins in Roman Britain', in Casey and Reece (eds.) 1974

coinage.t: The revolt of the mint workers at Rome
coinage.text: Early in Aurelian's reign the moneyers of Rome, led by the rationalis Felicissimus, rose in revolt. The sources say they had debased the coin (or embezzled silver) and rose when Aurelian moved to punish them; the fighting on the Caelian hill killed thousands of his soldiers (Aurelius Victor gives 7,000). Aurelian crushed them, closed the mint temporarily and later reorganised production: Rome's role as the dominant mint ended and new mints (Ticinum, Serdica, Cyzicus, Tripolis) took a greater share. The revolt helps explain the abrupt drop in quality around 270 and the urgency of Aurelian's reform of 274.
scholarship: Estiot, Monnaies de l'Empire romain XII.1 (2004)
Watson, Aurelian and the Third Century (1999)

coinage.standard: reformed radiate c. 3.9 g with c. 5% silver; marked XXI (KA in the East); aureus c. 1/50 lb
coinage.text: After reuniting the empire Aurelian issued a reformed radiate of improved weight and a guaranteed silver content of about 5%, marked XXI in Latin mints and KA in Greek ones (and occasionally XX). The meaning of the mark is still debated: 20 parts of copper to 1 of silver (1:20), or 'twenty units' (sesterces or nummi) to one coin, or a tariff of 20 asses. At Rome he also struck a laureate 'denarius' and some sestertii. The reformed coin carried new imperial imagery: Sol Invictus (ORIENS AVG), RESTITVTOR ORBIS, CONCORDIA MILITVM, and the dominus et deus titulature. All mints used officina letters and the XXI mark, creating the first empire-wide system of mint control marks. The reform did not stop inflation: papyri show prices rising after 274.
scholarship: Estiot, Monnaies de l'Empire romain XII.1 (2004)
Göbl, Die Münzprägung des Kaisers Aurelianus (1993)

coinage.standard: aureus c. 5.45 g; argenteus c. 3.4 g of fine silver; nummus c. 10 g with c. 4% silver
coinage.text: Diocletian rebuilt the coinage on uniform lines. A gold aureus at 60 to the pound (some marked Ξ, the Greek numeral 60) and a pure silver argenteus at 96 to the pound (some marked XCVI), in effect a return to Nero's denarius, headed a system whose workhorse was a large silvered bronze coin (c. 10 g, 27-28 mm), conventionally called the follis (its ancient name was probably nummus). A smaller radiate (no silver, without the XXI) and a laureate fraction completed it. The same reverse types were struck everywhere, above all GENIO POPVLI ROMANI (the Genius of the Roman people), and portraits became blocky and uniform, so that the four Tetrarchs are sometimes identifiable only by legend. Every coin carried a mint mark and officina letter. Alexandria's separate coinage ended. The 294 date rests on hoard evidence and the overall reform of mints; some components may have started earlier (the argenteus perhaps 293).
scholarship: Hendy, Studies in the Byzantine Monetary Economy (1985)
Abdy, 'The Tetrarchy', in Metcalf (ed.), Oxford Handbook of Greek and Roman Coinage (2012)

coinage.text: An inscription from Aphrodisias preserves an imperial edict, effective 1 September 301, that changed the face values of coins: on the usual reconstruction the argenteus was raised to 100 denarii communes (a unit of account) and the nummus to 25, roughly doubling their value. It warns that debts contracted before the change were to be paid at the old rates. A private letter on papyrus (P. Ryl. IV 607) shows someone rushing to spend 'Italian money' before it lost half its value, evidence that the change could also be a reduction for some coins. The currency edict prepared the ground for the Price Edict issued three months later.
scholarship: Erim, Reynolds and Crawford, 'Diocletian's currency reform: a new inscription', JRS 61 (1971)
Corcoran, The Empire of the Tetrarchs (2000)

coinage.text: Issued in November-December 301 in the names of all four Tetrarchs, the Edictum de pretiis rerum venalium fixed maximum prices for over a thousand goods and services in denarii communes: a modius of wheat at 100, a pound of pork at 12, a day's wage for a farm labourer at 25 plus food, a pound of gold at 72,000, a pound of purple silk at 150,000, sea freight rates by route. Its preamble denounces profiteers who raised prices where the army passed. Lactantius, hostile, says much blood was shed over trifles, goods vanished from the market and the law had to be abandoned. Fragments survive almost entirely from the Greek East (Aphrodisias, Stratonicea, Aezani and more than 40 other sites). For historians it is the richest single source on the late Roman price structure; for numismatists it fixes the relationship of gold to the unit of account.
scholarship: Corcoran, The Empire of the Tetrarchs (2000)

coinage.text: In the civil wars after Diocletian's abdication the nummus was repeatedly reduced, each ruler on his own timetable, so that coins of the same nominal value vary greatly in size between mints and years. Constantine's western reductions of 307 and 310 came first; Maxentius kept heavier coins for a time; Licinius' eastern IOVI CONSERVATORI coins (313-324) are small. Reverse types proliferate: SOLI INVICTO COMITI (Constantine's patron Sol, to c. 318-320), GENIO POP ROM, IOVI CONSERVATORI, MARTI CONSERVATORI, VIRTVS EXERCIT (with VOT XX standard, 318-320), BEATA TRANQVILLITAS (altar, 321-324). Weight, diameter and type allow fine dating, and these coins are cheap enough to assemble long chronological runs.
scholarship: King, 'The fourth century coinage', in King and Wigg (eds.) 1996

coinage.standard: 1/72 Roman pound (c. 4.5 g) of nearly pure gold
coinage.text: Around 309-310 Constantine, then ruling Gaul and Britain from Trier, began striking a lighter gold coin at 72 to the pound in place of Diocletian's 60. Its introduction in the West is dated by Trier issues; it spread to the East after the defeat of Licinius (324), when Constantine seized the eastern treasuries and confiscated temple treasures. The solidus became the most stable coin in history: it kept its standard for 700 years, was accepted from Britain to China, and gave its name to the soldier (soldato, soldier) and the 'sou'. Taxes were increasingly assessed and paid in gold (adaeratio), which pulled gold into fiscal circulation. Contemporary critics (the anonymous De Rebus Bellicis) blamed Constantine's gold for widening the gulf between rich and poor.
scholarship: Banaji, Agrarian Change in Late Antiquity (2001)
Depeyrot, Les monnaies d'or de Dioclétien à Constantin I (1995)

coinage.t: Late Roman silver: siliqua and miliarensis
denominations: siliqua (c. 3.4 g, reduced to c. 2 g)
coinage.text: Constantine reintroduced regular silver alongside the solidus. The coin conventionally called the siliqua (about 3.4 g, later reduced to about 2 g under Constantius II, c. 355) and the heavy and light miliarenses were mainly donative coins, struck for distributions to the army at accessions and anniversaries, which explains their vota legends (VOTIS V MVLTIS X). The names are modern matches with terms in the sources (siliqua as 1/24 of a solidus, miliarense as 1/1000 of a pound of gold) and the matches are uncertain. From the 360s silver carries PS (pusulatum, refined) in the mark. Siliquae were the main silver coin in Britain to its end and were clipped in the 5th century. Western siliquae of the Valentinianic and Theodosian houses with VRBS ROMA (Roma seated) and VIRTVS ROMANORVM are common; the miliarensis is scarce.
scholarship: Guest, The Late Roman Gold and Silver Coins from the Hoxne Treasure (2005)

coinage.t: VRBS ROMA, CONSTANTINOPOLIS and GLORIA EXERCITVS (330-341)
coinage.text: To mark the dedication of Constantinople (11 May 330) every mint struck two 'city commemoratives' in parallel: VRBS ROMA (helmeted Roma / she-wolf and twins) and CONSTANTINOPOLIS (Constantinopolis helmeted with sceptre / Victory on a prow), in vast numbers until 337 and beyond. Alongside, the standard type was GLORIA EXERCITVS with two soldiers and two standards (330-335), then with one standard (335-341), a reduction marked by a lighter coin. Small symbols in the standard (chi-rho, wreath, letters) distinguish issues.
