Collectors use these common coins to learn the late Roman mint system, since nearly every mint and officina can be collected.

coinage.t: How to read a late Roman mint mark
coinage.text: From 294 almost every coin carries in the exergue a mark built from (1) an optional prefix: SM (sacra moneta, sacred mint), P (pecunia) or M (moneta); (2) the mint abbreviation (TR Trier, LVG Lyon, ARL or CON Arles, R or RM Rome, AQ Aquileia, SIS Siscia, SIRM Sirmium, TS or TES Thessalonica, H or HT Heraclea, CONS Constantinople, N or NIC Nicomedia, K Cyzicus, ANT Antioch, ALE Alexandria, K or PK Carthage, T Ticinum, OST Ostia, LON or PLN London, AMB Amiens, MD Milan, RV Ravenna); (3) an officina mark, Latin in the West (P, S, T, Q) and Greek in the East (A, B, Γ, Δ, Є, S, Z, H, Θ, I, IA); and (4) field symbols or letters marking sub-issues. Precious-metal marks add OB (gold, obryzum, and the Greek numeral 72) or PS (silver, pusulatum). Traps: CON with a Latin letter in front is Arles; CONS with a Greek letter after is Constantinople; SMH is Heraclea, SMN is Nicomedia; COMOB on gold is used by many mints. RIC VI-X tabulate every mark.
scholarship: Sear, Roman Coins and their Values IV-V

coinage.text: Emperors took public vows (vota) for their own welfare at fixed intervals, discharged at quinquennalia, decennalia and vicennalia. Coins record them: VOT V (vows for five years taken), VOT X MVLT XX (ten-year vows fulfilled, twenty undertaken), VOT XXX MVLT XXXX. Because the vows were taken at anniversaries, often in advance, the numbers date coins to within a few years: Constantine's VOT XX coins of 315-320, Theodosius II's VOT XX MVLT XXX solidi with a long cross (c. 420-422), the VOT X MVLT XV of Arcadius and Honorius. Caveat: vows could be anticipated by a year or two, and junior emperors' vows ran from their own accession, which can mislead.
scholarship: Chastagnol, 'Les années régnales de Maximien Hercule', RN 1967

coinage.text: The coinage turned Christian slowly. Sol Invictus remained on Constantine's coins until c. 318-320; the chi-rho first appears as a small mark on the helmet of the Ticinum silver medallion of 315 and as a field mark in the 320s, and on the labarum piercing a serpent (SPES PVBLIC, Constantinople, c. 327). Constantine's posthumous coins (337) show him veiled and ascending in a quadriga with the hand of God reaching down: a hybrid of pagan consecration and Christian heaven. Magnentius made the chi-rho the whole reverse (353). Theodosius II's solidi with Victory holding a long jewelled cross (c. 420) put the cross at the centre; Tiberius II replaced Victory with the cross on steps (578); Justinian II's Christ portrait (692) falls after 641. The pace of change is a gauge of how cautiously emperors moved in public religion.
scholarship: Bruun, 'The Christian signs on the coins of Constantine', Arctos 1962

coinage.t: FEL TEMP REPARATIO (348) and the bronze reforms of the 350s
coinage.standard: large coin c. 5.3 g with a small silver content; reduced in 352/3 and again c. 355
coinage.text: For the 1,100th anniversary of Rome (348) Constans and Constantius II issued new bronze with the slogan FEL TEMP REPARATIO ('the restoration of happy times'), each denomination with its own type: the emperor dragging a barbarian from a hut, a phoenix on a globe or pyre, the emperor on a galley steered by Victory, and above all a soldier spearing a fallen horseman. Names such as maiorina and centenionalis come from laws in the Theodosian Code (title 9.23, on transport of money), and matching them to coins is uncertain. The falling horseman type became the standard eastern coin of the 350s, shrinking steadily, and it was copied massively in Britain and Gaul. Gallus Caesar's portraits and Julian's early Caesar coins belong to this series.
scholarship: Carson, 'The reform of the bronze coinage under Constans and Constantius II'

coinage.t: The Valentinianic reform of gold and silver (c. 366-368)
coinage.text: After Procopius' revolt (365-366), during which coins of doubtful purity were struck, Valentinian I and Valens tightened control of precious metals. Gold received in taxes was to be melted into bullion before reuse, refined gold was struck at mints that followed the court (the comitatus), and coins carried OB (obryzum, refined gold) and PS (refined silver). COMOB became the standard gold mark (COM for comitatus or the comes sacrarum largitionum, plus OB), and later CONOB for Constantinople. The reform helps explain why later 4th-century gold is so pure and why gold minting shifted with the emperors' movements between Trier, Milan, Sirmium and Antioch.
scholarship: Hendy, Studies in the Byzantine Monetary Economy (1985) 386-394

coinage.standard: c. 1.5 g (8 siliquae)
coinage.text: Introduced under Theodosius I (from c. 383), the tremissis replaced the 1.5-scripulum piece as the small gold denomination and became the dominant gold coin of the Germanic successor kingdoms of the West, where Merovingian, Visigothic and Lombard rulers copied it for centuries. Typical late Roman reverse: Victory advancing with wreath and globus cruciger, VICTORIA AVGVSTORVM; Byzantine tremisses show a cross. The 37 Merovingian tremisses of Sutton Hoo show the coin's long afterlife.
scholarship: Grierson and Blackburn, Medieval European Coinage I (1986)

coinage.t: The late Roman AE4 and the collapse of the bronze
coinage.standard: AE4 c. 1-1.5 g, 11-13 mm, falling below 1 g in the 5th century
coinage.text: From the 380s the main bronze became a tiny coin, SALVS REIPVBLICAE (Victory dragging a captive) and VICTORIA AVGGG, and after 395 the larger AE2 was abolished. The West stopped sending fresh bronze to Britain after c. 402, which is why Romano-British site finds end abruptly. In the 5th century, minimi of Leo I, Zeno and the Vandals, with monograms or a cross in a wreath, sank below a gram; one solidus was worth some 7,000 nummi by the end of the century. The reform of Anastasius (498) finally created multiple-nummus coins to make the small change usable again.
scholarship: Reece, The Coinage of Roman Britain (2002)

coinage.t: Clipped siliquae in late Roman Britain
coinage.text: Most siliquae found in Britain from the late 4th and early 5th centuries have had their edges clipped, sometimes so severely that the legend vanishes and the portrait is cut. Clipping went on after the flow of new coin stopped (c. 402-410) and seems to have been tolerated, perhaps systematic: it produced silver for imitations or for bullion while keeping the clipped coins in circulation. The Hoxne hoard, with over 14,000 siliquae nearly all clipped, is the main evidence, and the degree of clipping helps date hoards. Clipping was almost unknown on the Continent, which marks Britain's isolation in the last Roman decades.
scholarship: Guest, The Late Roman Gold and Silver Coins from the Hoxne Treasure (2005)
Abdy, 'After Patching', in Hunter and Painter (eds.) 2013

coinage.text: Large bronze medallions with a raised rim and a deep groove (contorno) around the edge, made in Rome in the later 4th and 5th centuries, perhaps as New Year's gifts or tokens connected with the circus games. They show emperors of the distant past (Nero, Trajan), Alexander the Great, Homer, Apuleius and charioteers, with pagan myths, circus scenes and the palm monogram (PE). Often linked with the pagan senatorial aristocracy of Rome (the circle of Symmachus), though the connection is debated. They are not coins. Rare, and copied in modern times.
scholarship: Mittag, Alte Köpfe in neuen Händen (1999)

coinage.text: Medallions were special issues outside the circulating system, struck from the 2nd century (Hadrian and the Antonines produced large bronze medallions, sometimes bimetallic with an orichalcum centre and copper ring) to the Byzantine period. Late Roman gold multiples (from 1.5 to 9 solidi and larger) were imperial gifts to officers and allied kings: the Beaurains (Arras) medallion of Constantius I, the Szilágysomlyó medallions of Valens, the 36-solidus medallion of Justinian (stolen from the Cabinet des Médailles in 1831 and melted; electrotypes survive). They carry ambitious iconography (imperial adventus, largitio scenes, triumphs) and are documents of court art and diplomacy.

Imperial women appear on coins in a sequence that tracks their public status. Livia appears anonymously (as Pax or Salus) and then named under Tiberius and as DIVA AVGVSTA under Claudius; Agrippina the Younger shares the obverse with Nero in 54; the Flavian and Trajanic women (Domitia, Plotina, Marciana) begin regular series. The Faustinas, Lucilla, Crispina, Julia Domna (with MATER CASTRORVM), Julia Maesa, Julia Mamaea, Otacilia Severa, Salonina and Severina carry dynastic and religious messages. In the 4th century Helena and Fausta (324-326) and later Flaccilla, Eudoxia, Pulcheria, Galla Placidia, Licinia Eudoxia, Ariadne and Sophia appear, often with the hand of God crowning them. The empress's crescent under the bust marks a double denomination in the 3rd century. Coins of empresses are a principal source for women's honorific titles (Augusta, Mater castrorum, Diva).
scholarship: Kleiner, 'Women and family life on Roman imperial coinage'
Brubaker and Tobler, 'The gender of money', Gender and History 12 (2000)

coinage.text: When an emperor or member of his family was deified, the mint issued commemoratives with DIVO or DIVVS and the symbols of apotheosis: an eagle (for an emperor) or peacock (for an empress) carrying the soul aloft, a multi-storey funeral pyre (rogus), an altar, a carpentum (ceremonial carriage) drawn by mules or elephants, the deified figure on a flying eagle. Decius' series of c. 250-251 restoring coins of eleven deified emperors (DIVO AVGVSTO to DIVO ALEXANDRO) and Claudius II's DIVO CLAVDIO coins (the most copied coins in Britain) are celebrated groups. The last pagan-style consecration issue is Constantine's (337), already infused with Christian imagery. Consecration coins are a primary source for the imperial cult.
scholarship: Gesche, 'Die Divinisierung der römischen Kaiser in ihrer Funktion als Herrschaftslegitimation'
Price, 'From noble funerals to divine cult', in Cannadine and Price (eds.) Rituals of Royalty (1987)

coinage.text: The successor kingdoms kept the Roman system. The Vandals at Carthage left gold to the emperor but struck silver and bronze with royal names and value marks (N XLII, N XXI, N XII). In Italy Odoacer and the Ostrogoths struck gold in the name of the eastern emperor, adding their own monograms on silver and bronze, and revived large bronze at Rome: 40-nummi pieces with INVICTA ROMA and the she-wolf, or an eagle, deliberately evoking the old sestertius. Theodahad's bronze with his own moustached portrait wearing a closed crown and Baduila (Totila)'s coins with his bust are rare exceptions to the convention of not portraying the king. These coinages are vital evidence for the political relationship with Constantinople.
scholarship: Grierson and Blackburn, Medieval European Coinage I (1986)
Metlich, The Coinage of Ostrogothic Italy (2004)

coinage.standard: first series follis c. 8-9 g (498); doubled to c. 17-18 g in c. 512
coinage.text: Marcellinus Comes records under 498 that Anastasius issued coins 'which the Romans call terunciani and the Greeks follares' and so made an exchange that pleased the people. He replaced the worthless nummus with multiples marked by large Greek numerals: M (40), K (20), I (10) and later Є (5), with the mint and officina below. After a first light series, the coins were doubled in weight around 512. The reform, partly anticipated by the Vandal and Ostrogothic coins of value, created the standard Byzantine bronze system and, by fixing the follis to the solidus, eased small transactions in the cities. Collectors date Anastasian folles to the light or heavy series by size and officina marks. It was part of a broader fiscal programme: the same year Anastasius abolished the hated chrysargyron.
scholarship: Metcalf, The Origins of the Anastasian Currency Reform (1969)

coinage.t: Justinian's dated folles and facing busts (538/9)
coinage.standard: follis increased to c. 22-25 g (538/9), reduced from c. 542
coinage.text: In Justinian's 12th regnal year (538/9) the follis became heavier and changed design: a facing bust of the emperor in helmet and cuirass holding a cross on globe, and on the reverse the value letter M with ANNO and the regnal year (XII, XIII...). Byzantine bronze is therefore dated by year from 538 to the 7th century. These massive folles, the largest Roman bronze since the 3rd-century sestertius, were reduced in weight from c. 542, probably owing to the fiscal shock of the Justinianic plague, and the reduction itself is visible year by year. The solidus also changed to a facing bust in the 530s-540s. Dated folles let collectors follow mint output year by year, a rare quantitative window on the 6th-century state.

From Justinian to the 7th century the Constantinople mint struck small numbers of solidi below the standard of 24 siliquae, marked in the exergue OB XX (20 siliquae), OB*+ (22) or with other signs (23). They are found mostly outside the empire, in Gaul, the Rhineland and Scandinavia, and their purpose is debated: trade with Frankish markets where gold was valued differently, diplomatic payments, or wages. Collectors should not confuse them with clipped coins or with Merovingian imitations.
scholarship: Adelson, Light Weight Solidi and Byzantine Trade in the Sixth and Seventh Centuries (1957)

coinage.text: Tiberius II replaced the Victory, or the angel holding a cross that had stood on the solidus since Justin I, with a cross potent set on four steps, often taken to represent the cross erected on Golgotha. It became the standard Byzantine gold reverse for over a century. Tiberius also restored more classical portraits and was later remembered for his generosity: chroniclers say he distributed vast sums and found treasure in the palace. The cross on steps lets a collector tell his solidi from those of Justin II at a glance.

In 615, with the Persians at Chalcedon, Heraclius introduced a large silver coin of 6 grammata (hence hexagram), with the legend DEVS ADIVTA ROMANIS ('God help the Romans') around a cross on a globe set on steps, and on the obverse the emperor with his son Heraclius Constantine. The Chronicon Paschale records that it was introduced in that year and that imperial salaries were thereafter paid at half their former rate in the new coin. In 622 Heraclius melted church plate to coin (Theophanes AM 6113), feeding the hexagram's production. It was struck in large numbers through the Persian war and into the reign of Constans II, then declined; it is the main Byzantine silver coin of the 7th century and a direct witness to the crisis that nearly destroyed the empire.

The war with Persia (602-628) and the loss of Syria and Egypt reduced the follis to a light, carelessly struck coin, very often overstruck on earlier folles (especially Phocas', whose memory Heraclius condemned) without removing the old design. Antioch closed in 610, Alexandria passed to the Persians (618/19-629), Thessalonica, Nicomedia and Cyzicus closed by c. 630, leaving Constantinople, Carthage, Ravenna, Sicily and Alexandria (after 629) as the working mints. Emergency mints at Seleucia and Isaura (615-618) show the front line. A typical Heraclian follis shows three standing figures (Heraclius, Heraclius Constantine, Heraclonas) with M and ANNO on the reverse; regnal dates continue but are frequently illegible.
scholarship: Hendy, Studies in the Byzantine Monetary Economy (1985)

coinage.t: Forgeries and how collectors detect them
coinage.text: Ancient coins have been faked since the Renaissance: Paduan 'Paduans' by Giovanni Cavino (16th c.) imitated sestertii and are now collected themselves; Carl Wilhelm Becker (1772-1830) cut hundreds of dies of rarities; 20th-century 'Slavey' and other Bulgarian workshops, Lebanese and Chinese factories produce struck and cast fakes of high quality today. Cast copies show soft details, pitting, a seam on the edge and low weight; transfer-die and struck fakes can be detected by die studies, by comparing with published die pairs (Crawford, RIC and specialist corpora), by fabric and flan shape, and increasingly by metallurgical analysis. Tooling (re-engraving a worn coin) and smoothing are more insidious frauds. Classic fake targets: EID MAR, Social War denarii, Caesar portraits, Judaea Capta sestertii, Otho sestertii (none genuine exist), Pertinax and Didius Julianus aurei, Uranius Antoninus, the Tetrici gold, Magnus Maximus solidi. Provenance and good references are the best defences.
scholarship: Klawans, An Introduction to Ancient and Medieval Counterfeit Coins (1977)

coinage.t: Aes rude and aes signatum: money before coins
coinage.standard: by weight; bars c. 1.5-1.8 kg (about 5 Roman pounds)
coinage.text: For most of its early history Rome measured value in cattle and sheep (pecunia from pecus, the Twelve Tables' fines in sheep and oxen) and in weighed bronze. Shapeless lumps of aes rude are found in votive deposits from the 6th century onward. Then came cast bars with designs, aes signatum: the earliest carry a 'dry branch' (ramo secco) pattern and are Etruscan and Italic; the Roman series (Crawford RRC 3-12) includes bars with an eagle and Pegasus, a trident and caduceus, shields, and the famous elephant/sow bar, often connected with Pyrrhus' elephants (280-275) and the story that pigs terrified them. These bars were valued by weight and frequently broken; the per aes et libram ceremony of Roman law (mancipatio with scales and a piece of bronze) preserves the memory of weighed money in classical times. Why it matters: Rome entered coinage late and from a bronze-weight economy, which explains the heavy cast as and the long dominance of bronze accounting (the sestertius, 'two and a half asses', remained the unit of account long after the as shrank).
scholarship: Burnett, Coinage in the Roman World (1987)

coinage.t: Aes grave: the cast libral as
coinage.standard: as of about one Roman pound (c. 270-330 g in different series); fractions marked by pellets (uncia = 1 pellet)
coinage.text: Rome's first official coinage was heavy cast bronze, aes grave, beginning in the early 3rd century (traditionally linked with the creation of the tresviri monetales, c. 289). The as weighed about a pound and its fractions were marked by value signs: S for the semis, four pellets for the triens, three for the quadrans, two for the sextans, one for the uncia. Early series show a range of deities (Janus, Mercury, Roma, Apollo, a wheel); the standard 'prow series' (Janus / ship's prow, from c. 225) fixed the iconography of Roman bronze for two centuries, and children in Macrobius' day still played 'heads or ships' (capita aut navia, Saturnalia 1.7.22). Cast coins were made in open or bivalve moulds and can show casting sprues. Parallel series were cast at allied centres (Luceria, Tuder, Hatria, Volaterrae). Identification: genuine aes grave has a granular cast surface with casting seams; most modern copies are lighter, too crisp, or have a sand-cast texture. Weight sequences are the key to dating them because the as was cut repeatedly: semilibral c. 217, sextantal c. 211, uncial in the mid-2nd century, semuncial in 91-89.

coinage.standard: Campanian didrachm c. 7.3 g
coinage.text: Pliny states that Rome first struck silver in 269 BC, in the consulship of Q. Ogulnius and C. Fabius, five years before the First Punic War. Modern scholarship accepts the date as a memory of a real event but disputes what it refers to: the Hercules / she-wolf and twins didrachm (ROMANO), the first silver struck at Rome itself rather than in Campania, or an antiquarian reconstruction. Pliny's further claim that the first silver was the denarius is now known to be wrong: the denarius is a creation of the Second Punic War. The Romano-Campanian didrachms struck before and after 269 were Rome's first silver, made for use in the Greek south, where coin had circulated for two centuries.
scholarship: Burnett, 'The coinage of Rome and Magna Graecia in the late fourth and third centuries BC', SNR 56 (1977)

coinage.standard: c. 7.3 g, falling to c. 6.6 g
coinage.text: Six or so issues of silver didrachms with matching bronze, struck on the Greek standard for Rome's dealings in the south. In probable order: Mars bearded / horse's head, ROMANO; Apollo / horse, ROMANO; Hercules / she-wolf and twins, ROMANO (the first appearance of the wolf on a coin); Mars / horse's head, ROMA; Roma / Victory with palm, ROMA; and Apollo / horse, ROMA. Their weight and style follow Neapolis; the issue sequence is reconstructed from hoards in southern Italy and from the change of legend from the genitive ROMANO (of the Romans) to the nominative ROMA. Bronze litrae with the same types accompany them. The didrachms are rare and expensive; the wolf and twins type is the most sought. Beware modern fakes from the 'Bulgarian' and Lebanese workshops: check style against Crawford and the die study in Burnett's work.

coinage.standard: c. 6.8 g, falling in weight and fineness after 217
coinage.text: The last and largest Romano-Campanian silver issue, named in antiquity after its reverse: Jupiter brandishing a thunderbolt in a quadriga driven by Victory, ROMA in an incuse tablet; obverse a beardless Janus head (the Dioscuri combined, or Fons, are other readings). Struck in great quantity from c. 225 to pay for the Gallic war (Telamon, 225) and the opening of the Hannibalic war. Under the strain of Trasimene and Cannae its silver content fell sharply, and it was replaced by the denarius c. 211. Livy mentions bigati and quadrigati in booty lists, and Pliny says the victoriatus and the quadrigatus were named from their types. Quadrigati were imitated in Italy and Sicily; heavily debased late specimens look grey and are sometimes plated.

coinage.standard: stater c. 6.8 g gold
coinage.text: Rome's first gold coins, struck around the crisis of Cannae (c. 217-215): Janus / two warriors swearing an oath over a pig held by a kneeling youth, ROMA in the exergue. The type, probably an image of a treaty sworn with Italian allies (the fetial rite of striking a pig with a flint), sends a message of loyalty at the moment when Capua and much of the south defected. A gold emission is itself a sign of emergency: Rome drew on the reserve of the aerarium sanctius. Extremely rare. The oath scene was revived by Ti. Veturius on his denarius of 137 and by the Italian rebels on Social War coins of 90.

coinage.t: The bronze crashes: semilibral and sextantal as
coinage.standard: semilibral as c. 135-160 g; sextantal as c. 54 g (one-sixth pound), struck rather than cast
coinage.text: The cost of the Hannibalic war forced repeated cuts in the bronze. Pliny connects a reduction with Fabius Maximus' dictatorship of 217 and claims the as fell to an uncia at that time; the coin evidence shows a two-step fall, to a half-pound (semilibral) c. 217 and to a sixth of a pound (sextantal) c. 211, when the as began to be struck instead of cast. The lex Flaminia minus solvendi of 217 has been associated with the reduction, letting the state pay debts in lighter bronze. The sextantal as is the bronze partner of the first denarius, tariffed at 10 asses, and the stratigraphy at Morgantina, which mixes early denarii with sextantal bronze, ties the two together. These reductions are the earliest documented case of Rome financing a war by changing its coinage.
scholarship: Marchetti, Histoire économique et monétaire de la deuxième guerre punique (1978)

coinage.standard: c. 3.4 g, 2.3 g, 1.1 g gold
coinage.text: A gold issue struck alongside the first denarii, with a helmeted Mars and value marks for 60 (the old fifty-sign with X), XXXX (40) and XX (20) in asses, and an eagle on a thunderbolt with ROMA. Valuing gold directly in bronze asses shows the new system in action: 20 asses equalled two denarii. The issue is usually linked with Livy's account of the emergency of 210 when senators contributed their gold and silver to the treasury. These coins are scarce rather than unique, and much faked; check weight, style of the eagle and the shape of the 60 sign.

coinage.standard: denarius 1/72 Roman pound (c. 4.5 g) of nearly pure silver, reduced within a few years to about 1/84 lb (c. 3.9 g)
coinage.text: In the darkest years of the Second Punic War Rome created a new coinage that would last nearly five centuries. The denarius (Roma helmeted, X behind her / the Dioscuri on horseback with lances, ROMA) was worth 10 asses, the quinarius 5, the sestertius 2½. It was struck at Rome and at several regional mints (L for Luceria, corn-ear for Sicily, and other symbols). The old view, based on Pliny, dated it to 269 or (Mattingly) to 187; Crawford's c. 211 is now generally accepted thanks to the Morgantina excavations, which found denarii in the destruction levels of 211, and to its consistent hoard sequence. The silver came from war booty and Spain; the denarius rapidly displaced the quadrigatus and in the 2nd century became the dominant silver coin of the Mediterranean as Roman spending grew. Why it matters: the denarius, its weight unchanged from c. 200 to Nero, was the instrument by which Rome paid its legions and absorbed the coinages of the Hellenistic world; in the Greek East it was equated with the Attic drachm.

coinage.standard: c. 3.4 g, three-quarters of the denarius weight but of lower silver
coinage.text: Struck alongside the early denarius: Jupiter / Victory crowning a trophy, ROMA. It carries no value mark and its fineness is lower than the denarius, so it is usually understood as a coin for trade with the Greek south and Illyria on the drachm standard, rather than part of the decimal denarius system. Pliny notes that it came 'from Illyricum' and was treated as merchandise. Struck in great numbers until c. 170, it then disappeared; its type was revived on the quinarius by the lex Clodia of c. 101, which explains why later quinarii show Victory with a trophy.

coinage.standard: denarius c. 3.9 g; as reduced to an ounce (uncial standard) or less
coinage.text: Pliny places the retariffing of the denarius from 10 to 16 asses under Fabius Maximus in 217, adding that soldiers' pay stayed at 10 asses to the denarius. The coins show otherwise: the value mark XVI appears on denarii of c. 141 (moneyers' issues dated by Crawford), followed by the star-shaped ligature ✳ (X crossed) used as the denarius sign thereafter. The change reflects the fall of the bronze as to an uncia or less. In practice the sestertius (now 4 asses) became the main unit of account, abbreviated HS (IIS), and all large sums in Cicero and the imperial sources are reckoned in sesterces. Identification: early 2nd-century denarii carry X; mid-century ones XVI; later ✳ or no mark.

coinage.t: From the Dioscuri to family propaganda
coinage.text: For two generations the denarius kept a fixed design (Roma / Dioscuri), with moneyers identified only by symbols or monograms (an anchor, a prow, a wolf's head). From the 190s variant reverses appear: Luna or Diana in a biga ('bigati', which Tacitus says Germans still preferred), Victory in a biga, Jupiter in a quadriga. From the 130s the moneyers, ambitious young nobles at the start of the cursus, turned the coinage into a medium for family history: Sex. Pompeius Fostlus (137) shows the shepherd Faustulus finding the twins; Ti. Veturius (137) revives the oath scene; C. Minucius Augurinus (135) the column of his ancestor; M. Marcius (134) the aqueduct of Q. Marcius Rex. This change in coin imagery coincides with the opening of the Gracchan era and the secret ballot laws, and has been read as an index of competitive aristocratic display before a voting public.
scholarship: Meadows and Williams, 'Moneta and the monuments', JRS 91 (2001)

coinage.t: Ti. Veturius: the oath scene denarius
coinage.text: Crawford RRC 234/1: helmeted bust of Mars (or a young warrior) with X / two soldiers touching a pig with their swords, held by a kneeling figure, TI VET and ROMA. Breaking with the Dioscuri formula, Veturius chose an oath scene that recalled both the oath gold of the Hannibalic war and, almost certainly, the shame of his relative T. Veturius Calvinus, consul in 321, who swore the peace of the Caudine Forks. In 137 the Senate was debating the repudiation of Mancinus' treaty with Numantia, which raised exactly the same question of a general's oath. A clear case of a coin type speaking to current politics.

coinage.t: Voting and liberty on the denarius
coinage.text: Late Republican moneyers repeatedly celebrated popular rights. P. Licinius Nerva (113/112, RRC 292) shows a citizen receiving a ballot and another dropping it in the urn on the pontes. M. Porcius Laeca (110/109, RRC 301) shows a magistrate, lictor and a citizen with the legend PROVOCO, the right of appeal guaranteed by the leges Porciae proposed by his ancestors. L. Cassius Longinus (63, RRC 413) shows a voter placing a tablet marked V (uti rogas, 'yes') in the cista, alluding to the lex Cassia tabellaria of 137. Q. Cassius (55, RRC 428) shows the temple of Vesta, the urn and a curule chair, recalling his ancestor's trial of the Vestals in 113. These coins are a primary document of the Roman voting procedure.

Denarii with notched edges were struck intermittently in the 2nd century and regularly between c. 118 and c. 64 (for example C. Mamilius Limetanus 82, Q. Antonius Balbus 83-82, L. Roscius Fabatus 64). The notches were made on the flan before striking. The traditional explanation, that they proved the coin was solid silver, fails because plated serrati exist. Tacitus says that Germans preferred serrati and bigati, old coins they knew. The best explanation remains open: a stylistic choice, a security feature that forgers quickly copied, or a marker of particular issues.

coinage.t: Plated denarii, Drusus' alloy law and the edict of Gratidianus
coinage.text: Plated denarii (fourrées: a copper core in a silver skin) were common in the late Republic; some were official. Pliny reports that the tribune M. Livius Drusus (91) 'mixed an eighth part of bronze into the silver', apparently a legal authorisation of a lower standard, and that the triumvir Antony later mixed iron into the denarius. In the chaos of the 80s, when good and bad coins circulated together, the praetor M. Marius Gratidianus (85) issued an edict establishing a public method of testing coins (ars probandi). It made him so popular that statues were raised to him in every vicus with incense and wine (Cicero, De Officiis 3.80); Sulla's men later tortured him to death. Collectors meet plated pieces regularly: a dark core showing at a break, a lighter weight, or a slightly blurry surface are the signs. Many ancient plated coins are themselves of historical interest and are collected as such.
scholarship: Lo Cascio, 'State and coinage in the late Republic and early Empire', JRS 71 (1981)

coinage.t: Lex Papiria: the semuncial as and the end of Republican bronze
coinage.standard: as of half an ounce (c. 13.5 g)
coinage.text: Pliny records that 'by the lex Papiria the asses were made semuncial'. The law is dated to 91 or 89. A few semuncial asses and fractions were struck in the 80s, then Rome effectively stopped striking bronze until Augustus. For two generations small change in Italy consisted of worn old asses, fractions of the Hannibalic war cut in halves, and local or foreign bronze. The gap shows how little the Republican state cared about small change compared with the silver that paid armies.
scholarship: Crawford, Coinage and Money under the Roman Republic (1985) 181-185

coinage.t: L. Calpurnius Piso Frugi and the control-mark denarii
coinage.text: RRC 340: laureate Apollo / naked horseman galloping with palm or torch, L PISO FRVGI. Struck in 90 in huge quantity to fund the Social War, it carries an enormous system of control marks (letters, numerals, symbols such as a lyre, anchor or crab), with more than a thousand obverse dies estimated. Crawford's die counts for this and similar issues are the basis for estimates of Republican coin production. Common, and a favourite of collectors who try to assemble control-mark sets.
scholarship: Hersh, 'Notes on the chronology and interpretation of the Roman Republican coinage', NC 1977

coinage.t: Coins of the Social War (ITALIA / VITELIU)
coinage.text: The Italian rebels' denarii imitate Roman weight and fabric but invert the message: Italia replaces Roma, and the Italian bull tramples the Roman wolf. Oath scenes swear the new alliance; some reverses show eight warriors, one for each confederate people. Legends in Latin and Oscan identify commanders (Q. Silo, C. Papius Mutilus 'embratur'). A unique gold aureus of Mutilus exists. Collectors should insist on provenance: these are among the most counterfeited Republican issues.
scholarship: Campana, La monetazione degli insorti italici (1987)

coinage.t: C. Mamilius Limetanus: Ulysses and Argos
coinage.text: RRC 362: bust of Mercury / Ulysses returning home in traveller's garb, greeted by his old dog Argos. The Mamilii of Tusculum claimed descent from Telegonus, son of Ulysses and Circe. One of the most charming Republican types and a standard example of mythological genealogy on coins; struck on serrate flans.

coinage.t: L. Titurius Sabinus: the Sabine women and Tarpeia
coinage.text: RRC 344: bearded head of King Titus Tatius with SABIN / two soldiers each carrying off a woman (the Rape of the Sabines) or Tarpeia buried to the waist under shields. The moneyer's family claimed Sabine origin, and the issue, struck during the Social War, flattered the Sabines at a moment when Rome needed loyal Italians. His descendant was the Q. Titurius Sabinus killed by Ambiorix in 54.

On campaign in the East and on his return to Italy Sulla struck coins under his own authority as imperator, including the first substantial issues of Roman gold since the Hannibalic war: L SVLLA IMPE ITERVM with the jug and lituus (symbols of the augurate) and two trophies, and L MANLI PRO Q (his proquaestor L. Manlius Torquatus) with Sulla in a triumphal quadriga crowned by Victory. These coins, produced by military mints that moved with the army, foreshadow the generals' coinages of the civil wars. Sulla's aurei are rare; the denarii are scarce and widely copied.

coinage.t: Q. Pomponius Musa: the Muses series
coinage.text: RRC 410: a punning set of ten reverse types, Hercules Musarum playing the lyre and each of the nine Muses with her attribute, with the head of Apollo (or of the Muse) on the obverse. Hercules Musarum refers to the temple of Hercules of the Muses built by M. Fulvius Nobilior after 189, which housed statues of the Muses from Ambracia; the coins may copy those statues. Completing the set is a classic collecting challenge, and the Urania and Hercules types are the rarest.

coinage.t: M. Aemilius Scaurus: King Aretas and the camel
coinage.text: RRC 422: struck by Scaurus and P. Plautius Hypsaeus as curule aediles, with REX ARETAS and the Nabataean king kneeling beside a camel offering an olive branch, a boast of Scaurus' campaign against Petra in 62 while serving under Pompey. Josephus says Aretas actually bought peace for 300 talents. Combining a foreign king's submission with aedilician games propaganda, it is a vivid example of late Republican self-advertisement. Common.

coinage.t: Faustus Sulla: Bocchus hands over Jugurtha
coinage.text: RRC 426/1: diademed Diana / Sulla seated on a raised seat, with Bocchus kneeling before him offering an olive branch and Jugurtha kneeling with his hands bound, FELIX. It reproduces the gilded group that Bocchus dedicated on the Capitol in 91, which so enraged Marius (Plutarch, Marius 32), and celebrates the moment in 105 when Sulla, as Marius' quaestor, secured Jugurtha's surrender: the origin of the feud between the two men. Faustus, Sulla's son and Pompey's son-in-law, struck it while backing Pompey.

coinage.t: M. Junius Brutus as moneyer: Brutus and Ahala, LIBERTAS
coinage.text: The future assassin, as moneyer in 54, struck two types: head of L. Junius Brutus (first consul, expeller of the kings) / head of C. Servilius Ahala (who killed the would-be tyrant Sp. Maelius in 439), linking his father's and mother's ancestors; and head of Libertas / the consul Brutus walking between lictors preceded by an accensus. Struck while Pompey's dominance was being discussed, they read in hindsight as a manifesto of tyrannicide. Scarce in good condition.

RRC 448/2: bearded, long-haired male head with a chain around the neck and a Gallic shield behind / naked Gallic warrior hurling a spear from a biga driven by a charioteer. Often called a portrait of Vercingetorix, then a prisoner in Rome awaiting Caesar's triumph (46), it is more probably a generic captive Gaul; a companion type shows a Gallic woman with dishevelled hair and a carnyx. It is the closest the coinage comes to the Gallic war that made Caesar.

RRC 443/1: elephant trampling a serpent or dragon (often read as a Gallic carnyx), CAESAR / pontifical implements (culullus, aspergillum, axe, apex). Struck in enormous quantity in 49-48 from the treasury Caesar seized in Rome, it paid his army in the war against Pompey and is the commonest Republican denarius. The elephant may pun on 'caesar' (said to mean elephant in Punic, Historia Augusta, Aelius 2.3) or symbolise victory over evil; the reverse proclaims his position as pontifex maximus. Abundant ancient imitations and modern fakes; genuine pieces have a slightly irregular, round flan and the elephant's trunk raised.

In January-March 44 the moneyers M. Mettius, L. Aemilius Buca, P. Sepullius Macer and C. Cossutius Maridianus struck denarii with the head of the living Caesar, a step no Roman had taken at the Rome mint. Legends trace his escalating titles: CAESAR DICT QVART, CAESAR IMP, CAESAR DICT PERPETVO (from February 44), PARENS PATRIAE. On some he wears a wreath of the kind the senate voted him, and some issues show him veiled as pontifex. The issue sequence, reconstructed from dies, is the closest thing we have to a week-by-week record of the months before the Ides. Collectors pay heavily for good portraits; worn and holed examples are common, and so are fakes.

coinage.t: EID MAR: Brutus' Ides of March denarius
coinage.text: RRC 508/3: bare head of Brutus, BRVT IMP and L PLAET CEST (the moneyer L. Plaetorius Cestianus) / a pileus (the cap of a freed slave) between two daggers, EID MAR. Struck by a travelling military mint in Greece or Asia in 43-42 before Philippi, it is one of the few Roman coins described by an ancient writer: Cassius Dio says Brutus put on his coins 'his own likeness and a cap and two daggers, showing by this and by the inscription that he had freed the fatherland with Cassius'. Around 80-100 silver specimens and three gold aurei are known. It is the most famous and most forged ancient coin; every specimen should be checked against published die pairs (Woytek and others). The irony of a tyrannicide placing his own portrait on the coin was not lost on contemporaries.
